speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of extreme urgency. News from the United States has revealed that the environmental protection agency of that nation proposes in a draft document a repeal of air pollution standards which restrict acid rain, and suggests that decisions regarding pollution control be left to individual states. In light of the fact that such a move would have disastrous consequences here in Canada and, if approved, would have to be considered a deliberate rejection of last year's bilateral memorandum of agreement concerning trans-boundary air pollution, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the government immediately contact the United States administration to protest strongly the proposed loosening of air pollution standards and declare its intention to take legal action, if necessary, to prevent such changes.

Given the fact that the government of Quebec operates under authority delegated to it by the Fisheries Act and the Minister of Fisheries by virtue of the 1923 agreement, and given the reply to my colleague from the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, has the minister satisfied himself that the Quebec government has acted prudently in terms of the conservation measures it is now enforcing in Quebec? If not, what steps does the minister propose to take to exercise the authority which is his and which, in this particular case, he has delegated to another government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subtopic: ACTION TAKEN BY GOVERNMENT OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, although I have been here a number of years I did not delegate the authority. It has been done by order in council since 1922. We have not tried consistently to second guess the authorities in the province of Quebec. I said so publicly, and I want to say it again. Generally the province of
June 23, 1981

Quebec has administered those fisheries with a considerable degree of wisdom and conservation. There are some areas, outside the salmon issue, where we found that Quebec tended to stretch the extent of its jurisdiction. In fact in some cases I had to indicate I did not find acceptable certain attitudes vis-a-vis licensing or implications for fishermen from other provinces.
The question of the salmon is an extremely difficult issue because it is a fairly short season. When there are incidents such as there are now, it is very often difficult to pacify the situation before the salmon run has either escaped those who are entitled to catch it or it has been hurt by over-fishing.
The province of Quebec has taken an attitude on the salmon fishing which has been slightly more harsh than the attitude I have taken. For example, it did not reopen the fishery to commercial fishermen. That was its right to decide under the present legislation. I did not wholly agree with that position. However, I cannot on one hand agree to the delegation of authority and, on the other hand, do the day-to-day management over somebody else's shoulder.
My colleague and I are re-examining the implications of the 1922 agreement as it is presently applied. We will review this. If we come to the conclusion that it should be changed or altered, then we will do so according to the tradition, that is, by order in council.

subsubtopic: MR. ANDRE-PROPRIETY OF SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order respecting supplementary estimates (A) that were deemed to have been reported last evening and from which will arise an appropriations bill this Friday. I talked to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) about this particular period, and he agreed that this would be an appropriate time to raise the matter.
Supplementary estimates (A) are very simple in that they consist of a single item, namely the energy program of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. The estimates contain two separate money items. The first is vote 20a, which is described as follows:
-Payments to refiners and other importers of crude oil and petroleum products for the purposes of Part IV of the Petroleum Administration Act- $2,143,300,000.
Then the second part is a statutory item entitled "Petroleum Compensation Revolving Fund" in a negative amount of $2,143,300,000, which is identical to the amount in vote 20a. Therefore the net budgetary expenditure is zero, because one has been netted against the other or has been subtracted.
Further in the estimates there is an explanation of the requirement which shows that increased oil compensation payments require the additional $2,143,300,000. Then there are increased revenues to the Petroleum Compensation Revolving Fund in that amount. Thus it is a negative amount of $2,143,-
300,000.	Then there is an explanation of the objects of expenditure in the amount of $2,143,300,000, less increased revenues of the same amount. The net expenditure is supposedly zero and the net requirement is supposedly zero.
I believe these estimates, particularly the item entitled "Statutory", the Petroleum Compensation Revolving Fund, are out of order and inappropriate for these estimates for three reasons. In fact, I believe the estimates as presented are false in terms of what they are supposed to be. They are misleading and out of order according to the precedents and standards required of estimates, as indicated by decisions of Your Honour's predecessors and as set out in Beauchesne's fifth edition.
I believe there are three separate reasons why the item is out of order. First, the statutory item is not an expenditure; it is a revenue item. In fact it is described further on in the estimates as increased revenues in the amount of $2 billion, as well as "Less: Increased Revenues" of $2 billion. On two occasions the item is described as a revenue item. The estimates are intended to present to Parliament the spending program of the government, not its revenue program.
The revenue program is handled in a different manner. It is handled through taxation and presented to the House in the form of a public account at the end of the year in terms of total revenue. However, during the course of the year we have other sources of information from the government as to its revenue intentions. The estimates are not intended to indicate revenues.
I should like to bring to the attention of the Chair Section 484 of Beauchesne's fifth edition, page 169, under the section entitled "Estimates", wherein the following is indicated:
The purpose of the estimates is to present to Parliament the budgetary and non-budgetary expenditure proposals of the government for the next fiscal year. These estimates include Votes, which Parliament is asked to approve through Appropriation Acts, as well as other items called statutory items, for which the required expenditures have already been approved through existing legislation and are included only for information purposes.
Very clearly, according to Beauchesne's fifth edition, the estimates are supposed to include only expenditure items-two types, votes requiring an appropriation act, and "statutory" where there is an existing legislative authority. They are not intended to include revenues for which some legislative authority might exist.
Section 487 on the same page of Beauchesne's fifth edition reads as follows:
(1) The Estimates are limited to setting out only the sums which it is calculated will be required in the current year,-
It is just a reinforcement of Section 484 in terms of the intention of the estimates. I maintain that, as a result of this being a revenue item and not a spending item, that statutory item should be ruled out of order.
June 23, 1981

My second and additional reason why this statutory item is out of order has to do with the purpose of the petroleum compensation revolving fund. The supplementary estimates do not contain a description of what the purpose of the fund is but the main estimates for 1981-82 do. I refer the Chair to page 7-32 of the main estimates. There the objective of the petroleum compensation revolving fund is defined in this way:
To provide incentives for the development of designated classes of high-cost domestic petroleum through the payment of compensation to first users of such petroleum-
In other words, the petroleum compensation revolving fund is for the purpose of subsidizing or making payments to users of high cost domestic petroleum-not imported petroleum but domestic. Further evidence is contained on page 7-34 of the main estimates and, indeed, may be found in Chapter 34 of the Adjustment Accounts Act as well as Chapter 72(4) of the Petroleum Administration Act.
It is very clear that the statutory authority for the petroleum compensation fund is to subsidize domestic high-cost petroleum. At present Syncrude is the only one to fall into that category, with oil produced from the tar sands in Northern Alberta. If you look at vote 20a, Madam Speaker, it clearly states that it is for the purpose of "payments to refiners and other importers of crude oil and petroleum products for the purposes of Part IV". My point is that this estimate nets off the petroleum compensation fund, which is a revenue item, from vote 20a, the moneys required to subsidize imports. It is an inappropriate mixing. Vote 20a deals with the subsidization of imports. The statutory item deals with the subsidization of Syncrude oil produced in Canada.
They are apples and oranges. It is inappropriate to suggest that on the one hand, since we require a dozen more apples, we can subtract the dozen surplus oranges we have and reach a net requirement of zero fruit. They are not the same thing; they are two different items. I submit that it would be equally inappropriate for the government to take corporate taxes and in the estimates subtract those from fiscal transfers to the provinces, for example, and therefore say that the net spending on fiscal transfers in this new figure. They are two different items; they do not belong on the same side of the ledger paper. Even if they did by some peculiar reasoning, you should not subtract the two anyway because they are different items.
My third reason for submitting that that statutory item is out of order has to do with the fact that the item is itself anticipatory. In fact, there is no legal authority for the amounts contained therein. I refer the Chair to Citation 484 of Beauchesne which states:
These estimates include Votes, which Parliament is asked to approve through Appropriation Acts, as well as other items called statutory items, for which the required expenditures have already been approved through existing legislation and are included only for information purposes.
Clearly, a statutory item must be backed up by existing legislation. Even if the statutory item was a true expenditure, as opposed to a revenue item, it would be out of order for inclusion because the necessary legislation allowing the gov-
Point of Order-Mr. Andre
ernment to raise these funds has not yet been passed. Indeed, the necessary amendments to the legislation have not even been introduced.
I refer the Chair to notice of ways and means motion from Votes and Proceedings of July 11, 1980, and also to notice of ways and means motion of June 2, 1981, which is a notice of ways and means motion to amend the Petroleum Administration Act in a way which would provide the authority for the government to collect those revenues which would go into the petroleum compensation fund, which is supposed to be used to subsidize synthetic crude oil. The ways and means motion has not been introduced or voted upon in this House. Nor have there been amendments to the Petroleum Administration Act.
Indeed, yesterday the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) tabled in the House a document entitled "Discussion Draft of the Energy Security Act 1981". Contained therein are those provisions which would give the statutory authority to collect the moneys which are indicated as being in the supplementary estimates as a negative expenditure, whatever that is. So there really is no legal authority yet for that measure.
You will recall, Madam Speaker, that when this issue was first raised on July 11, 1980, we on this side of the House raised a point of order having to do with the appropriateness of using a notice of ways and means motion for this particular device. It really is not a tax, it is a revolving type of fund. At that time Your Honour ruled that this was a legal question beyond the competence of the Chair and inappropriate for the Chair to decide upon. Subsequently we sought legal advice on this matter and were advised that, in fact, it was illegal. We were also advised that were we to pursue the matter we would be achieving a pyrrhic victory, since all that would be required would be for the government to pass retroactive legislation, which is what is being done in this energy security bill.
The language in that proposed legislation shows on page 22, I believe, that the provisions will become effective on July 10, 1980. This is an indication that some time in the future an act will come before us which will apply to a period about a year and a half ago, which will give statutory authority to an item which is placed into these estimates, subtracted from another item. So there is net spending even though they are apples and oranges and even though it is inappropriate to have revenue items in the estimates in the first place, since the estimates are supposed to talk about expenditures.
For all of the reasons I have set out, Madam Speaker, I humbly submit to you that it would be appropriate to request the government to strike out this item. It does not affect the government's appropriations. We will not have to sit here all summer while remedial action is brought in. The net effect will be to put the supplementary estimates in order, making the information contained therein accord with the rules as established by Beauchesne and Your Honour's predecessors. I believe this will contribute to a better understanding of what is being spent, what is being raised, and how many apples and oranges we have as opposed to the mismanagement that we see.

Madam Speaker, there seems to be some confusion in the mind of the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) with respect to what is intended by supplementary estimates (A). Last night I commended the hon. member as a chemical engineer having turned his hand to law, but I will have to qualify that commendation this afternoon.
If you look at the vote in question, vote 20a, essentially it seeks additional spending authority under Energy, Mines and Resources, vote 20. Energy, Mines and Resources, vote 20, called for payments to refiners and other importers of crude oil and petroleum products for the purposes of Part IV of the Petroleum Administration Act of $3,015,400,000. The purpose of supplementary estimates (A) is simply to increase that amount in the amount indicated, namely, $2,143,300,000.
Madam Speaker, one does not vote statutory items. The statutory item which appears beneath that, the petroleum compensation revolving fund, is inserted for the information of hon. members, to show that if and when legislation is adopted, there will be a netting of these amounts. Because it is the intention, as indicated by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), to create a fund which will be net. However, at the moment this is not the case, and no one is seeking that to be the case. We are simply seeking additional authority to extend the further amount for the same purposes, namely, payments to refiners and other importers of crude oil and petroleum products for the purposes of Part IV of the Petroleum Administration Act.
If one looks to the contribution at the bottom of page 2 of the estimates, one will see that increased payments to refiners and other importers of crude oil and petroleum products is expressed as a gross amount of $2,143,300,000. Therefore, I suggest to Your Honour that the hon. member for Calgary Centre has not understood the purpose of showing netting, which is done for information and factual presentation to hon. members of this House. speechtext: What is the jurisdiction of the proposed new gulf region in Atlantic Canada and where will the headquarters be located?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subsubtopic: ATLANTIC CANADA-PROPOSED GULF REGION
speechtext:
The gulf region will encompass all of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, extending in the north to include the Strait of Belle Isle and in the south to a line extending from Cape North Nova Scotia to the Ramea area on the south-west coast of Newfoundland. subsubtopic: ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS-CONTROLS
speechtext:
1.	What was the estimated number of immigrants illegally in Canada for each year 1975 to 1980?
2.	What mechanism or method of control does the government employ to monitor the entrance and exit of visitors and immigrants to Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS-CONTROLS
speechtext:
1. There is no way of estimating the number of persons illegally in Canada.
2. There are no exit controls for immigrants or visitors leaving Canada. All persons seeking entry to Canada are examined on the primary inspection line and those whose intent or purpose is judged questionable are referred to immigration for further consideration.
Those visiting for over three months are documented on the form IMM. 1097. Others visiting for under three months may also be documented on IMM. 1097 at the discretion of the examining officer. Those with approval to work here for a specified time in a pre-arranged job are documented on the form IMM. 1102 and overseas students intending to attend school here must complete a form IMM. 1208.
All immigrants are documented on their visa and landing records on form IMM. 1000, which is retained as a permanent record of their permanent residence status in Canada.

speechtext:

subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT

speechtext:
The House resumed from Monday, June 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Blais that Bill S-10, to amend the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
Corporations and Labour Unions

subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we rose last evening to vote on the very important Bill C-57,1 had just begun my remarks on Bill S-10.
I see the minister is in the House. So that he does not think that all we in the opposition do is criticize, I must congratulate the minister on two or three counts. First of all, the short title, which has come to be known as CALURA, has a kind of exotic and almost intoxicating ring to the name. I think that it is an interesting way to put together a bill so that one can come up with an acronym which makes it sound exciting.

subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Credit for that goes to John Diefenbaker.

subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
However, when one looks at the bill, it is anything but intoxicating. It is a very long and very complicated piece of legislation, even though the pages are very short.
I would also like to congratulate the minister on a couple of matters in the bill. First of all, he raises the threshold under which corporations are required to report. I think that is a welcomed part of the bill. In addition to that, apparently it will be easier to consolidate statements, and therefore easier for corporations to comply with the regulations under that bill.
However, having said that, as might be expected I think there are a lot of concerns that we have relating to the bill. It bothers me that there is really no justification given as to why we need some of this information and regulation. What I think does concern all of us in this country, which is a very large country, is that the government should take into consideration collecting some of the information that it needs in conjunction with some of the provincial governments. I can give the minister an example which I hope he will take into consideration, and I hope we raise it at committee.
The province from which I come, Manitoba, is now in the process of revising, or has just revised, the Manitoba agricultural lands protection act. This is an act which is in place to protect the lands of Manitoba from being purchased by foreigners; at least, people who do not choose to reside and work on the land. The minister stated that one of the purposes in the bill, as reported at page 10707 of Hansard of June 17, is as follows:
-there is presently no system which can indicate the level of technological transfers from Canadian corporations to foreign interests or vice versa.
It seems to me that, in addition to talking about technological transfers, the minister is also interested in finding out how foreign corporations operate in this country in terms of ownership. One of the things which could assist the government, and which could also cut back on the amount of paperwork required by individual corporations at the same time, would be for the federal government to set an example and try to work with the provincial governments in areas where the provincial governments would be involved in gathering the same kind of data the federal government is interested in under this bill.

subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
They will be using this data. We have arrangements.

June 23, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions

subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The minister says they will be using this data. It seems to me that this is a suggestion which can be used by both the federal government and the provincial governments in the sense that everyone should be working together to see that when information is collected, it is collected for a purpose and in such a way which is the least painful and therefore the least expensive to the people from whom that information is being extracted.
I checked with the Manitoba government this morning to find out if there had been any co-operation or any indication that this bill was coming forward at the provincial level, so that when there are bills passed which will be collecting the same kind of information from the residents of Manitoba or, for that matter, any other province in Canada-after all, a citizen of Manitoba or a citizen of Prince Edward Island is also a citizen of Canada-that both levels of government do what they can to see that this information be collected in the most inexpensive and expeditious way possible.
It seems to me that this would do a couple of things. It would lessen the cost to the individual who is collecting this information. By the way, in some cases when this information is collected the responsibility of providing the information falls on some of the chartered accountants. I have had conversations with accountants who find it very difficult, in some cases, to comply with the requests which come from the Department of National Revenue. I suspect the same criticism would apply to whoever is collecting this information, in the sense that information is asked for and it has to be charged against the accountant's time. He really cannot bill it back to the individual client per se. Therefore, what results is that the over-all level of charge which the accountant must put on his customers has to be raised. That is something I would hope the minister would take into account. I am pleased to see that he is in the chamber this afternoon.
Very briefly, as I do not particularly want to take a long time, I have two or three concerns which I want to( raise. One of the concerns, which I think has been expressed previously, is that we are in the process of developing a very large system of paper burden in this country. As an example, I do not know whether I will get a hernia from lifting this bundle of paper I have in my hand, but this is the kind of regulation which is in front of this House. This is the number of bills which are in front of the House.
I think we have to be careful to see that the regulations and laws we pass do not become excessive. Some time ago I read that the first five-year plan in Russia weighed several tons! The small business community in this country is concerned that the information collected be relevant and useful.
Early in the session I had a letter from a constituent about the monthly ES-1A report, which reads in part as follows:
We have been sending this report for over a year and we have only twenty-one (21) employees.
Who is benefiting other than a few statisticians who can say they bamboozled the Government to allow a 100 per cent sample?
As a result of that letter I wrote to the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) expressing my constituent's concern, specifically asking him if he could give some reason for the information being collected. I received a reply which I appreciated but unfortunately it did not give me any specific reason except to say that in the public sector the information is used by such agencies as the Bank of Canada, the system of national accounts and the Department of Finance in the determination of fiscal and monetary policy. That is a very heady reason for collecting information from a firm that employs only 21 people. I think this example illustrates that the government should see to it that the paperwork for small business does not become burdensome.
Clause 4 of the bill deals with the return to be filed with the Chief Statistician of Canada by corporations and labour unions. It seems ridiculous to take one quarter of the 16 pages of the bill to set out the information that the government is asking for. Clause 19 provides that the governor in council may make additional regulations.
I hope that we can take these matters into consideration when the bill is considered in committee to make sure that the information gathered is used.
Through technology, methods are available that would allow us to collect weather information at one-foot intervals between Ottawa and Edmonton. The amount of this information would be horrendous, and simply because it is possible to collect it is no real reason for doing so. It seems to me that this is the kind of labyrinth of paperwork that could result from this bill, which devotes four pages to enumerating the information that will be required.
Then, in addition, another section sets out the kind of information that the governor in council may require. We really do not know the purpose for which the information is sought.
It was pointed out earlier that a lot of federal government agencies and provincial governments collect basically the same kind of information. If we need all this information, and I am not sure that we do, then surely we should see that it is collected in the least expensive way possible.
Those are the concerns that I have with the bill, Mr. Speaker. Last night, the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) suggested that the bill should be withdrawn and a more straightforward one brought forward. Perhaps some of the recommendations of the task force on government regulations that reported to the House last fall could be adopted. That all-party committee came up with some interesting and useful ideas about government regulations and information. The government should take its recommendations seriously and, if it does not withdraw this bill, should allow major amendments to the bill when it reaches committee.

subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too wish to express my concern about some parts of this bill which has been with the Senate since December, 1980 and now, within weeks of adjourning for the summer recess, for some reason it has acquired urgency. That is apt to make
June 23, 1981

members on this side a little more suspicious than they would ordinarily be.
My colleagues have spoken at length about some reasons why they find the bill more repugnant than it would appear at first glance. Their points have been well made and I should now like to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, some points made by members of my constituency, businessmen who feel that they are overburdened by government regulation. I have with me three letters from businessmen in my constituency who have asked that I not use their names. They have a justifiable fear that the information the government is continuously seeking from private companies and information compiled on the daily lives of individuals may lead to some form of recrimination. I am not sure that such a thing would happen, but they think they have a justifiable concern and they express it by their wish to conceal their identity.
A corporation is asked to provide its name, address of head office, the manner in which the company is incorporated, the amount of authorized share capital, the number of shares, description of voting rights and the number issued. This information is already available to the government so there is no need to burden taxpayers and the corporations that contribute to the wealth of the federal government through taxes with more paperwork. As a matter of fact, I understood that this government was committed to lessening the burden of paper work on corporations, but I do not think that Bill S-10 will accomplish that. A question put to the minister by the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), which is reported at page 10859 of Hansard, reads as follows:
Could the minister tell the House whether any evaluation was made during that study of what is the cost of complying under the act for business and for consumers throughout Canada? Is there some estimate as to what it is costing businessmen to comply with the act as it now exists, and can the minister give us any estimate as to what it will cost businessmen to comply with the new act if it is passed in its present form?
The minister replied:
I do not have with me any information in terms of the total cost to an individual company of completing a form on an annual basis. However, I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that it would not appear to be a concern of any of the companies with whom we have had exchanges.
The government has imposed an additional cost of doing business upon private corporations, yet the minister has no idea how much it will cost them. I think if he had concern for his portfolio and the corporations for which he is responsible, he could find out how much it could cost them to complete the forms he has requested. After all, he has the resources of a department at his disposal.
The bill also requires trade unions to furnish the name and address of each employer resident in Canada with which it has a collective agreement, and the number of male and female members in the local union. I do not understand what differ-
Corporations and Labour Unions ence it would make to the government whether a trade union member was male or female. I do not see that as information which this government would not be able to exist without. It requests the total number of employees covered by the collective agreement and the balance sheet, showing the assets and liabilities of the union. That information is already available. It is available to members of the unions and it is available in other forms to this government.
A statement of income and expenditures is also requested. In addition, a financial statement with respect to each special fund of the union is requested. If I were a union member, I would be very suspicious of the government, or of anyone else, who requested information which showed what I had in my strike fund and so be able to see how long the union would be able to last, how long I would be able to stay on strike and how long members would be able to be fed and clothed. I do not see any other reason for the government to be requesting this information unless it is to make judgments as to how long the government could expect work stoppages to continue and how flush the union strike funds are.
There is a clause in this bill asking international unions to make a statement containing amounts paid or credited to the union in the reporting period. I do not understand the necessity for this information. Again, information is requested about expenditures made by the union and recorded as being directly related to its operations in Canada. This information is available. It is not something which has been withheld from governments in the past. It is not something that any responsible union tries to withhold. The information is available. But now we have a bill, apparently very urgent, which the government wants to have passed asking the trade unions to comply in this manner.
On reading the speeches made in connection with this bill and the speech and interventions made by the minister, I find that he was the only speaker, to my knowledge, on that side of the chamber. He was not content to be the only speaker, but he continued to interject while other members were speaking. His interjections were on spurious points of order pertaining to who brought in the bill originally and why. I would think that if government members wish to partake, they could ask the minister responsible to share a little bit of time with them, giving members opposite the opportunity to discuss this bill in the House.
It has been said by other members that this bill does not seem to do anything productive. The bill does not add anything to productivity in Canada.
When companies and labour unions are filing returns, there should be some guarantee that these returns will be kept confidential.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief. I thank the hon. gentlemen who have spoken this afternoon for their contributions.
I am sure when the bill gets into committee they will help greatly. However, I want to bring precision to some of the comments that have been made in the spirit of attempting to clarify some issues, so that we will be knowledgeable as to what this bill is about when we are in committee.
Basically this bill is a statistical one. It was deemed necessary as early as 1962 because of Canada's particular position vis-a-vis the United States, the large number of subsidiary companies existing within Canada, the large amount of foreign investments and the great number of international unions in Canada. Because of these things Canada needs a system to collect information and therefore know exactly the extent of foreign investment and how many international unions are operating within the country.
This was not a bill initiated by a Liberal government. It was initiated in 1962 by Mr. Diefenbaker, who was prime minister at the time. I have been advised by those in the House during that period that it was basically a cornerstone of his policy on economic nationalism and it was strongly supported by the Tory members of the government at that time. I am very pleased that initiative was taken and brought forward.
What we are attempting to do is to remove some of the amendments which were made in 1965 by a Liberal government in order to simplify the process. The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) indicated in his intervention that what we were proposing would create some disadvantage or some problem for international unions in terms of their reporting. Quite to the contrary, what we are attempting to do is to put more fairness in to the reporting system so that international unions will be able to report more of the expenditures they are making for the benefit of members of Canadian unions who belong to an international organization.
In effect, what has developed is a report which was filed in 1977. In that report we saw a $45.4 million deficit. In other words, more money was going to the United States than was coming back into Canada in terms of the exchanges between the locals of international unions which operated within Canada.
As we are now preparing the amendments and as we are proposing in this bill, we will be permitting international unions to show a much more realistic picture of the money flowing into the United States or to the international unions from Canadian locals and also how much money is being invested by international unions in services and benefits available to members of Canadian locals. I trust those comments will, in some way, permit the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood to review the provisions of this bill so that he can make his contribution in committee.
Yesterday we heard the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) make an issue of the colour of the various forms that were attached to the former legislation, or the legislation that I am seeking the consent of the House to amend. It is true that they are multicoloured. The argument he was making was very helpful to the case to be made by the government in the sense that, of the eight forms that he was mentioning, we are combining those eight forms into one basic form that will have to be filed by the corporations under the corporations returns portion of the bill.
In effect, the forms that he was referring to yesterday were not only Statistics Canada forms. There were also two forms that are required by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce which will no longer have to be filed with that department by the corporations. I am referring to questionnaires Nos. 3 and 4. The information that was sought by these questionnaires will be included within the major universal form that is contemplated under clause 4 of this bill.
The hon. member for York-Peel made a strong case about the quarterly surveys required of various types of corporations by Statistics Canada. Each of these surveys applies to a different sector of the economy. All corporations do not have to file all eight of the multi-coloured forms. Quite the contrary; each corporation belongs to an industrial sector and there is a special form for that sector.
What is to happen now is that one of the quarterly reports will be included within the consolidated form. Because these are quarterly surveys there will be an ongoing obligation on
June 23, 1981

the part of the corporation to file three other quarterly reports as previously required by Statistics Canada.
I would like to assure hon. members that this is not a regulatory bill. That is a misconception. There is nothing regulatory in this legislation. We are attempting to provide authorization to collect information, not to regulate it. It is quite clear that the purpose of the total information we require is not to regulate but to permit the Government of Canada, and indirectly the governments of the individual provinces, to adopt certain policies that are in the provincial or national interest.
So much for the forms. I will now deal with the question of technology transfers. I am surprised that members opposite did not comment more on that aspect of the bill because it is new. As I said in my opening remarks, there are no provisions at the provincial or federal levels where national statistics can be obtained in terms of technology transfers.
One of the major factors to be taken into consideration in terms of future economic development is access to technology. Every developing nation, middle nation and developed nation is very jealous about being able to obtain and guard its technology in order to foster its technological development. Canada has had the major advantage, as a result of having a large number of multinational subsidiaries within Canada, of having access to the technology being developed by the parent company. That is a major advantage.
There is also a requirement for our own national development and the future of international trade for Canadians that we in Canada know what sort of technology has been transferred to Canada and what sort of intentions there are in terms of developing technology within Canada so as to create a better and wider industrial and manufacturing capacity within this country. There is a recognition that, without our being able to seize upon and develop our own technology, we will not be able to develop an international capacity in trade. Basically what we will be doing is requiring companies in Canada to identify for us not the nature of the technology nor the substance of the technology that is being transferred, but the arrangements for the technology transfers that are made between companies outside and within Canada.
I wear different hats as Minister of Supply and Services. One of the major thrusts of my ministry in terms of minister of supply is to use every procurement dollar in order to improve Canada's capacity in the manufacturing sector. As the report that was tabled yesterday by the task force on the National Trading Corporation shows, in 1980 we had an $18 billion deficit in end products. That was $1 billion more than in 1979. I am led to believe that in the very near future it will be over $20 billion in end products. Therefore, we as Canadians have an obligation to reduce that deficit. We will only be able to do that if we create a better Canadian manufacturing capacity.
Within my ministry I am using every procurement dollar as best 1 can to encourage the Canadian private sector to develop additional Canadian capacity. Recently I announced the source development fund. It is there to try and create addition-
Corporations and Labour Unions al Canadian manufacturing capacity, the potential of which is identified as a result of the procurement process.
I have within my department what we call the unsolicited proposals fund, $20 million a year. It is not a large amount of money. I wish I could have $40 million or perhaps $50 million. The purpose of that unsolicited proposals fund is to encourage the development of Canadian technology, encourage the private sector, increase research and development efforts to create new technology and new marketable products, not only for the Canadian marketplace but the international marketplace. The secret behind everything I do is to try and identify technology.

A technology that we could develop and improve in Canada not only to meet Canadian requirements on the Canadian market but also those of the international market. That is why I support this bill and am very anxious to have it passed because we will then have some knowledge, which we do not have now, at the level of technology transfers from multiona-tionals and other sources to Canadian branches as well as from Canadian corporations to other foreign companies. It seems to me that it is actually a major need in our economy, and I am quite surprised that no member opposite has said that it is essential for Canadians to have such information and that indeed the only way to obtain them was to use Statistics Canada, a most efficient tool not only in Canada but throughout the world.

Statistics Canada is the agency that will be collecting all the information that is required under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act.
With those very brief statements, I hope that this bill will now proceed to committee where we can have a very intelligent debate on the contents of it. I have indicated to members of the opposition that I am open and flexible in terms of amendments that they may wish to present so long as they fit within the bill and the intentions I would like to espouse. Having said that, I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members for their attention.

subtopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT

speechtext:
that Bill C-66, to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs,
He said: Mr. Speaker, this short bill is primarily intended to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act so as to clarify the power conferred upon the Superintendent of Insurance to incur certain expenses in exercising control of a company for its rehabilitation or in carrying out its winding up under the provisions of the Winding-up Act.
The provisions of the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act prescribe that when a company is experiencing financial difficulties the Minister of Finance may give the Attorney General of Canada the responsibility of seeking from a superior court an order authorizing the Superintendent of Insurance to take control of the company for its rehabilitation or winding-up pursuant, as I just said, to the Winding-up Act. Section 113 of the act, which will be clarified by the bill which we are studying now, provides that when the superintendent takes control of a company for its rehabilitation or winding-up, the expenses incurred in exercising that control must be paid by some or all of the insurance companies registered under this act or under the Foreign Insurance Companies Act.
The payments made by the industry to cover the expenses thus incurred by the superintendent in managing the operations of a company for its rehabilitation or winding up will ensure that the assets of the company which is experiencing financial difficulties will be used solely to settle the claims of its policyholders.
The federally chartered Strathcona General Company, which had to face outstanding claims of roughly $39 million, had financial difficulties earlier this year. It will be remembered that the Supreme Court of Ontario ordered the superintendent to assume control of the company for its financial rehabilitation, and a project aimed at enabling the company to meet its obligations was drafted by a consortium representing certain sectors of the insurance industry and other interested parties. In order to see this project through, the consortium agreed to underwrite a bank loan so that the company would have enough funds for its cash requirements and thus be in a position to pay off its claims while it would attempt to recoup the money it had loaned out. It was agreed that the interest on that loan would be an integral part of the expenses incurred by the Superintendent of Insurance in exercising control of the company for its rehabilitation.
Payment by the superintendent of the interest on the money borrowed by the company and the subsequent sharing of these costs by the industry seemed to go much further than the spirit
of the legislation, under which the superintendent is authorized to do all that is necessary to allow the company under its control to meet its commitments for rehabilitation purposes. At the present time, when winding up the company, the term all "the expenses incurred" is mentioned in the act. However, in spite of the intent of the law, the Department of Justice believes that the present wording of Section 113 is such that the payment of interest and other costs as well as the expenses shared by registered companies could be questioned.
The bill aims therefore at eliminating any doubt concerning the power of the Superintendent to pay, at the time of the rehabilitation or winding up of the company, the interests on loans obtained to meet the cash requirements of the company as well as the costs of terminating the leases or employment contracts or other similar expenses. The bill also amends Section 113 of the Act to establish clearly that when the expenses are incurred in respect of a company which transacted only the business of property and personal risk insurance, only premium income from this category of insurance shall be taken into account to be shared in by companies. Mr. Speaker, this is not a very thick bill. However, as you can see, it is of major importance. I have had discussions with representatives of both opposition parties, and it seems that we could refer the bill to the committee of the whole and then proceed to third reading. This is what I hope will happen, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I was wondering when the changes were to be made to the wording of the Order Paper regarding this particular bill. I am glad the minister has made the proposal and the House has accepted the suggestion that we go from second reading to the Committee of the Whole.
One might ask how on earth it is that at this stage of the session such a bill can have such priority, not only within the cabinet pecking order but within the pecking order of the House. This is a housekeeping bill required to clear up some doubt in the Department of Justice about what you and I would consider to be proper expenses in the liquidation of an insurance company, including interest costs on money borrowed by a consortium. Such a change is necessary in somebody's mind regarding this aspect of the ordinary liquidation of the assets of a company in order to pay off some creditors.
June 23, 1981

Sometimes one has to wonder about the thinking of the Department of Justice. This is the sort of bill which always gives me cause for doubt, just as I have doubts when a minister of the Crown says he has been advised by the legal officers of the Crown that certain bills or certain proposed steps are quite in order. Then I say yes, but what about things like Bill C-66? Little wee doubts are expressed for what you and I, Mr. Speaker, would agree are perfectly legitimate purposes. On reading the act we are mystified as to why the proposals were brought forward. Well, if the Department of Justice is wrong on this particular little wee peanut bill, how can they be right on major issues? This is precisely the type of situation we face.
The ultimate purpose of this bill, of course, is perfectly reasonable. There is no doubt in my mind that if an insurance company should get into trouble the superintendent has the power to organize a syndicate to liquidate the affairs of the company in order to save the creditors from unnecessary losses. He has the power to pay certain expenses which ultimately, if there is a deficiency of assets, are chargeable against the industry. There will in no way be a charge against the public purse.
However, what is he entitled to include in those expenses which the industry will ultimately have to pay? Naturally one would have thought that interest costs on funds borrowed by the consortium in order to keep the company going for a time so that it can be liquidated in an orderly fashion would be an appropriate expense. However, somebody raised a doubt about it so this is why we are into this sector.
The insurance company in question was in this local area and that may be what has prompted the government to get on with this bill and put it into this timetable. The shareholders or participants in this company are no different from anyone else. They merit no more consideration than anyone else. As a matter of fact, I think they were gullible to the point of being negligent. They thought they had a free ride to profit.
This company which went into liquidation was frankly nothing but a reinsurance broker. When they got into trouble and efforts were made to get the industry to bail them out, the industry said: "These people came out with ridiculous rates on ridiculous terms, they undercut us, and now you ask us to bail them out. Have you got a hole in your head?" And quite rightly so. I am absolutely astounded at some of the major reinsurance brokers in this country-and I will be charitable beyond all reason by not using their names-who placed large amounts of insurance with this company simply because the rates were low. They should have known better. It was an open secret in the industry that all Strathcona was doing was engaging in some frantic reinsurance, laying off, and just skimming through the commissions. That is all they were living on, the reinsurance commissions.
Well, on a couple of rather major claims that did arise the reinsurance people abroad simply told them to take a flying jump and to take their chances on legal proceedings. In other
Insurance Companies
words, they simply said lump it. Of course, the game was over and that is all that has happened.
Now, that having been taken care of, the question is: which costs of cleaning up this mess can be properly charged against the assets? Ultimately the residual will be paid by the industry, and that is all we are dealing with this afternoon. There is not one cent of public money involved, otherwise I think we would have had a great deal more to say. However, I am in agreement that the public trustee should not be put in a position where he has to counter an opinion from the Department of Justice as to what expenses he can authorize in an orderly liquidation. It is not only a matter of interest costs, but it is the cost of liquidating any leases which might exist.
This points up one final factor. It may be that in this case, where not too many people are going to get hurt, certainly not the public, we and the superintendent should take a look at the requirements of those people filing a proposal for a licence as a federal insurance company. I think there has to be a tightening up here. We have to look at the industry. The insurance industry in this country is predominantly owned-even more so than some sectors of manufacturing or those involved in the exploitation of minerals-and operated by foreign interests. Canadian investors have been notorious in their reluctance to organize into responsible general insurance firms. There are over 300 companies involved in general insurance, a handful of which are Canadian. There is no way that the Government of Canada is going to say: look, we are going to institute statutory requirements that those people in the insurance business in Canada shall comply with, like the banks, newspapers and broadcasters; Canadianize by saying that no more than 25 per cent of any insurance company will be owned by foreign interests.
There is no market. No Canadians are willing to buy. That is the state of the market. There is no money around. I do not care what political party wants to espouse Canadianization, there is nothing in the law which will force investors to buy interests from foreign insurance companies under any circumstances.
The answer is not public ownership. God help us if we fall into that trap. There is no way that either the federal government or the provinces can become successfully involved in the general insurance business. Those attempts at becoming involved in the general insurance business are now a disaster as far as policyholders are concerned.

Quebec. I think there is a tremendous tendency, which is quite natural on the part of any group of individuals who are responsible for the administration of something which has gone wrong, to say, "We did all we could in the circumstances; there is nothing more we can do. We admit no responsibility for what has gone wrong."
In addition to the need for an inquiry into what happened, there is a need, in my view, for a clarification of exactly what the responsibility is of the Superintendent of Insurance and of the government. The superintendent is there as a representative of the public when something has gone wrong. Obviously this is a question which will be settled by the courts.
The minister of consumer and commercial relations indicated at Queen's Park yesterday that the activities of Re-Mor were directly and intricately linked with the activities of Astra, that Astra was serving as a front for Re-Mor and vice-versa. In those circumstances the question we must ask ourselves is: What is the meaning of the federal licence? What is the consequence of the granting of a federal licence and what is the responsibility of the government to those individuals who rely on the granting of a federal licence? The minister has consistently answered the question by saying that it is a provincial responsibility when it comes to Re-Mor. I do not accept that answer. I do not think the court will accept that answer either. Time alone will tell.
With respect to those investors who put more than $20,000 into Astra, that is a question which strikes directly at the heart of the federal obligation. It involves the question whether there is a responsibility on the part of the federal government, when it grants a licence and when it supervises the licence, to see that individuals are not taken in by the mere granting of a licence but that the licence itself has some meaning, in addition to the simple principle of an individual being insured up to $20,000.
Does this mean that, no matter what the government knows and no matter what information it has with respect to the conduct of those companies, it has no additional responsibilities and its only responsibility is the $20,000 liability? Or, in the instance of the insurance companies act, which is what we are dealing with, are we saying that the liability of either the industry or the government with respect to the activities of the Superintendent of Insurance is strictly limited to what is specifically set out in the statute? Or are we saying, is there not some additional obligation on the part of the federal government to inform investors, potential savers and policy holders, if there are some questions in their minds or if they have some information which has come to them with respect to the companies involved?
I say to the minister that were the members of the Liberal party from Ontario in this House as concerned as their counterparts in Queen's Park, we would have some answers to these questions. In the province of Ontario we really have a one party state. We have the natural governing party, the Tory party, and we have the same party federally, the Liberal party. It just goes by a different name. We are suffering.
Insurance Companies
I see the minister shaking his head. This is absolutely true. I have correspondence in my office from people all over southern Ontario in their seventies and eighties who have lost thousands of dollars, and in some cases tens of thousands of dollars, their life savings, because of what has happened to Re-Mor and Astra Trust. They have not received a single answer to any of their questions from either their federal or provincial government. If Liberal party members in this House from the province of Ontario were prepared to be as vigilant in this House as those in Queen's Park, we would have some answers, because the minister would have to provide those answers.
There are several questions. How is it that this company was allowed to get a licence when there were so many questions posed over five years about the characters, the abilities and the qualifications of the principals involved in that company? There was a pattern of political interference, both at the provincial and at the federal level, from both provincial and federal politicians, which was referred to in the report of the standing committee on justice in the provincial legislature when there was a minority government in Queen's Park. How is it that the questions about that have simply been brushed aside by the minister?
How is it that as soon as the company Astra Trust was incorporated, it was allowed to engage in investments which were contrary to the Trust Companies Act, which were contrary to the Ontario securities act, and which were known to the Superintendent of Insurance?
I wrote to the minister concerning the breaches of the Ontario securities act. When my letter was answered by the Superintendent of Insurance, I asked him, "When you knew there were breaches of the Ontario securities act, why did you not do anything about them?" He said, "We are not responsible for breaches of provincial legislation". I have that answer in a letter from the Superintendent of Insurance replying to a letter which I wrote to the minister. I am telling the minister that that answer is not satisfactory. In this realm of trust companies and in the whole financial field, there is something very wrong indeed if the answer of someone who is responsible for the administration of the federal government is simply, "It is in someone else's ballpark; we are not responsible for that".
One would like to know, and one would have to have an inquiry to know-and there needs to be an inquiry to know- what communication there was between the Superintendent of Insurance and the Ontario Securities Commission. When they wanted that information at Queen's Park, when they had the select committee on justice meeting, the minister said, "No, we are not going to allow the Superintendent of Insurance to even appear before that committee." There has been one meeting of the finance committee in which we had an opportunity to question the Superintendent of Insurance. That was not any kind of an investigation. Indeed, I am not particularly keen on the idea of having partisan politicians engaged in a crossexamination of the people who are involved in a search for evidence. I am not interested in that. However, I am interested

June 23, 1981
Insurance Companies
in knowing that a judge will be asking those questions and will be looking at those documents. He will be asking the question of the Superintendent of Insurance, "What were your contacts with the provincial authorities and with the Ontario Securities Commission?"
That is not a witch hunt and it is not looking for unfounded allegations. That is looking for some very specific answers to some very specific questions. I say to the minister that if there were, indeed, no contacts, and if, indeed, it was over a year before the Superintendent of Insurance was aware of the existence of Re-Mor, the provincially incorporated company, the question is, "What is wrong with our method of supervision that this was allowed to happen?" That is not a witch hunt question. That is a very specific question which has nothing to do with whether or not Mr. Carlo Montemurro was or was not a crook. Whether Mr. Montemurro was a crook, or whether the people associated with him were crooks, is a question which will be settled in the criminal courts of this country.
However, whether there was something wrong in the way in which the Government of Canada supervised the conduct of these companies is not a question of criminal activities on the part of people who are associated with the companies. That is a very separate question. Individuals who have been involved, who have invested, who have tried to save, and who have taken a risk have done so because they assumed there was a guarantee of some kind, even if they were not exactly sure what the nature of that guarantee was. The question of what is the responsibility of the governments of Canada and Ontario to these people is not, I would respectfully submit to the minister, a question of the individual taking the government to court, because that would be a very expensive, lengthy, protracted and difficult proposition for a number of people who do not have a lot of money. It is not a question of the private obligation between the Government of Canada and Mr. "X" or Mrs. "Y", whoever the investors happen to be. It is not a question of a purely private obligation. It is a question of the public obligation of the government with respect to the supervision of companies for which it has responsibility, for the bona fides of which it is making some kind of claim in the sense that it is granting them a licence and that licence has some kind of a meaning.
Because it is a question of public obligation, I am disturbed that the minister has gone back on the commitment he made to the committee that the government would publish and abide by the report of a group of lawyers who were trying to arbitrate this question of the responsibilities of the governments of Ontario and Canada with respect to investors in Re-Mor and Astra Trust. I say the minister has gone back because there was a very real difference between the answer which he gave me at the end of the hearing in the committee, which he will recall, and the answer which he gave me in the House some two weeks ago, when he simply went back to the old argument of the government instead of the strict legal argument which, in my view, will not eventually hold much water. The strict legal argument is, "It is not our responsibility; we are not responsible for Re-Mor; Re-Mor and Astra Trust are two separate companies, and we are not going to do anything for people other than the $20,000 responsibility which we paid and accepted because of the insurance provisions".
I say to the minister that the answer which he gave in the House is, in my view, going to prove wrong when it comes to the end of the day. However, more important than that, there is no reason why the people who have suffered as the result of the collapse of these companies should have to wait that long, should have to pay that much money in legal fees, and have to suffer that long before the government recognizes that it has some obligation to them.
I do not pretend to have all the answers to the questions I have raised. I have tried to make the questions, which I have raised at some length with the minister in letters to him, as specific as possible. Frankly, I am not concerned with any kind of witch hunt with respect to the activities of anyone who is responsible for the supervision of these companies. I am concerned with two very basic questions. How is it that a licence was granted and that the company was allowed to conduct itself for so long when the government knew that something was wrong? Second, why will the government not recognize that it has a responsibility to those people who have put their faith in the seal of approval, which is what a federal charter means? I say to the government that there are profound reasons in our political culture why these questions are not resolved. They have to do with the fact that we live in two one-party states in this province, the one-party state of Canada where we have perpetual government and a perpetual Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and the one-party state of Ontario where we have the same problem. That is the reason these questions are not raised.
Despite that, this amendment is a minor one. We want to know why Strathcona was allowed to operate in this instance, what actual damages have been suffered by some people and how they are being compensated. These are questions which will not be resolved by this housekeeping legislation.
Rather than seeing a bill like this one brought forward at the present time, I think it would make more sense for the government to say that something is wrong. This is the first time we have seen the collapse of a federally-incorporated trust company since the depression. Why did it happen? The criminal charges have been laid; but the question of how this could have been allowed to go on for so long, whether the government could have done something about it and whether the government will need extra power where it suspects such things are going on, are questions that will not be resolved by a criminal trial. They will not even be resolved by a civil trial between the government and individuals who seek compensation. Such questions can only be settled by a judicial inquiry. That is the only way we will find out how a licence came to be granted and what the relationship or communication was between the federal and provincial governments. I think the
June 23, 1981

public ought to know the answers to these questions and that the minister ought to know them as well. I say to the minister, with great respect, that answers have not been forthcoming about the collapse of this company, and in my view they should be.
I will have some specific questions for the minister when the bill is in Committee of the Whole about the activities of Strathcona and the activities of the superintendent with respect to Strathcona. This party is concerned about the principles of superintending and supervision, and about the principles of insurance as they relate to the liability of investors and policyholders who put faith in the idea that the government was supervising and superintending the matter. These more fundamental problems lie behind my remarks today and I hope the minister will take them in that context.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will answer the first question as to whether the people who were insured will sustain losses as a result of the decision made by the office of the Superintendent of Insurance to proceed with the financial rehabilitation of the Strathcona Insurance Company. With the assistance of a consortium, no individual, no group or no corporation that was insured will sustain losses on amounts owed to them for risks covered by Strathcona.
As to the background of corporate difficulties, which is a much broader question raised by the hon. member, may I say that in 1979 the auditors from the office of the Superintendent of Insurance became aware that the company was beginning to sail on rough seas. From that moment on and on a regular basis, the superintendent's office would dispatch its auditors to make sure that the company would be taking corrective action. Company management did make some commitments but, unfortunately, they were not respected. When those facts came to light in January, 1980, the superintendent submitted a report to the minister who decided to renew the company permit for a limited time, that is until March 31, 1980, advising company management that they had to meet the requirements set for them by the Department of Insurance.
In May, 1980, a new president of the company was appointed and several changes were made, but as the problems of the company were known on the market, it could not attract enough new customers to ensure more receipts and thus improve its financial position. In short, Mr. Speaker, that is what happened.
I think there are two major factors which were raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). First, there is a basic defect at the management level which must be directly related to the rate fixing policy of the company. Secondly, there is a blatant lack of will to restore quickly the financial position of the company. However, under the plan proposed by the superintendent to rehabilitate the corporation

State Immunity Act
with the assistance of a consortium, as I indicated in my first answer to the question, no policyholder will lose money as a result of the problems experienced by the company. I must also say that the reinsurance of the company with some foreign companies has also contributed to its financial problems. I have asked the Superintendent of Insurance to look fully into the manner in which insurance companies operating in Canada provide reinsurance and to suggest how the existing legislation might be improved so that insurance companies operating in Canada and dealing with foreign reinsurance companies would have firm guarantees with respect to the quality, solvency and soundness of these reinsurance companies.
