subsubtopic: IMMUNITY OF FOREIGN STATES IN CANADIAN COURTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a bill for the clarification of the law and the
better protection of Canadians and others who may find some	HH
day that they have a claim in Canada against a foreign	HH
government. The problems this bill is designed to resolve are	HH
that, at best, the present state of the law is quite uncertain concerning the legal responsibility of foreign states in Canadi- ^H an courts, and, at worst, the law may be too protective of foreign governments and cause injustice to people in this country who suffer injuries or loss at the hands of foreign HH states operating in Canada.
What has developed in Canada is a tradition going back	HH
almost to the divine right of kings. The monarch was too	HH
dignified to be sued. This followed into the state and the state	^H
in relation to other states. This has changed significantly.	^H
What has happened in Canada is that the provinces and the federal government have made themselves subject to court action, like the ordinary citizen. Second, governments are ^H deeply involved in commercial activity by their agents all around the world.
The growth and penetration of commercial activities carried on in Canada today by agencies of foreign governments makes it increasingly important that we have a law on this subject ^H which is clear and fair to all. What happened historically with ^H our important trading partners, for instance the United States, HH is that in 1952 the United States took this absolute immunity right and changed it by informal agreements in informal meetings. In 1974, the United States passed a foreign sover- ^H eign immunities act. In 1972, the Council of Europe adopted a ^H convention codifying restrictive immunity. In 1978, Great HH Britain, a signatory to that convention, followed suit by pass- ^H ing the state immunity act of 1978.	^H
Because we do not have any law, what has happened in	^H
Canada is that quite a bit of confusion exists in the minds of	^H
the public and in the minds of the courts. For example, in the	^H
Democratic Republic of Congo v. Venne, (1971) Supreme	^H
Court Reports, at page 997, the Supreme Court of Canada	^H
confirmed the absolute immunity of states. Then the appellate	^H
court of Quebec did not follow this ruling in Zodiak Interna-	HM
tional Products Inc. v. Poland. 81 Dominion Law Reports,	H|
Third Edition, at page 656.	^H
We would like to make it clear to the public, the average Canadian, who is dealing with a foreign country or its agents what to expect in the end regarding the collection of debts or the type of actions that can be pursued.
Bill S-19 was discussed in the other place. Witnesses were called, the provincial attorneys general were canvassed and their opinions were sought. I do not want to go into every clause of the bill but I would like to make some references.
In clause 2, "commercial activity" has led to some discussion. There is the English example which defines commercial activity in great detail. This has led to certain problems because of the large amount of detail. The English courts from our observations have tended almost to disregard their definition, which was too broad. The Americans, on the other hand, have a narrow definition of commercial activity, leaving it up
June 23, 1981

to their courts to decide what is and what is not commercial activity. We have adopted the American example in our proposed bill and will leave it up to the courts to decide what is commercial activity.
In general terms, there is to be no immunity of foreign states operating in Canada from any proceeding relating to any commercial activity of the foreign state, clause 5; any proceedings relating to death, personal injury, damage to or loss of property caused in Canada by a foreign state, clause 6; actions concerning ships or cargo involved in commercial activity, clause 7; actions concerning property received by a foreign state through succession, gift, etc.; clause 8; proceedings for injunctions, specific performance, etc.; against separate agencies, no matter whether the agency is engaged in commercial activity or not, clause 10(3); execution against a separate agency, clause 11(2); other than when military property is involved, clause 11(3).
A procedure for the service of documents is set out. It is hoped that we do not run into examples such as Corriveau v. Cuba which involved damage to the Cuban embassy. There was a landlord and tenant relationship; there was a default and judgment was obtained. Another example is Edwards v. U.S.S.R. which involved the seizure of a Soviet vessel. There was a great deal of confusion on the part of the litigants as to what rights did or did not exist.
In conclusion, I am sure my friends across the way will have a great deal to say about the merits of the bill. It is hoped that by following the example of European conventions, Great Britain and the United States, we in Canada will be able to codify basically protection for the average citizen when dealing with a foreign nation. In the 1980s we do not think that the theory of the divine right of kings or the presumption of infallibility of the state should be followed. What we have in Canada is a collection of individuals from abroad who are operating in this country in order to earn profit. They should have no greater or lesser rights than the citizens of Canada in their dealings.

subsubtopic: IMMUNITY OF FOREIGN STATES IN CANADIAN COURTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this momentous bill in this full chamber with some trepidation-

subsubtopic: IMMUNITY OF FOREIGN STATES IN CANADIAN COURTS
speechtext: After great study.

subsubtopic: IMMUNITY OF FOREIGN STATES IN CANADIAN COURTS
speechtext:
-after great study and consideration of the provisions of this bill. I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will agree with me in this connection. This place astounds me and mystifies me at the same time.
Just a few days ago the government in full dirge went ahead with its motion of closure with respect to Bill C-57. One would have thought that the economic future of Canada depended upon moving on with economic bills, that if Bill C-57 with respect to excise tax did not pass, the economy would stop and the country would stop in its tracks. Therefore we had an emotional, heated debate at that time as to whether closure should be invoked. Some felt it was an important matter and that the economy should be discussed in this House in the last few days before the summer recess.
State Immunity Act
As soon as the closure motion passed, the first items of business the government brought forward were such outstanding bills as the so-called CALURA bill, the bill dealing with the Canadian and British Insurance Companies and now a bill dealing with diplomatic immunity. I wonder aloud as to where the great urgency was on the part of the government with respect to rushing through and curtailing debate on an important economic bill, one that affects the lives of virtually every Canadian. The government cleared the decks so that we can spend two or three days talking about the question of diplomatic immunity, as important as that is.
I appreciate very much the learned dissertation of the parliamentary secretary as to the content and purpose of the bill. However, people might get the impression from the comments made by the distinguished parliamentary secretary that somehow this bill is going to codify and advance the rights of litigants and citizens of Canada with respect to being able to enforce judgments against foreign powers and representatives of foreign countries in Canada.
While I have to admit I agree with the parliamentary secretary that the bill does go a long way in codifying the present law, there are still some very serious questions with respect to how the bill will be interpreted in the courts, and the extent to which the rights of Canadians to sue, receive judgment and realize on that judgment against foreign states or their agencies will be advanced by the provisions of this bill.
One might get the impression from the title of this bill that it extends the right of diplomatic immunity while operating in Canada. Quite the contrary; it is an attempt to codify and set forth in statutory form the provisions, rights and limitations on diplomatic immunity, the rights of foreign countries to carry on so-called commercial activities in our country and the extent to which they are going to be held responsible with respect to contracts, tort liability or damages to Canadian citizens in the course of carrying on their commercial activities. There is an attempt here to specify the limitations which are placed on foreign countries represented in Canada and their agents.
The parliamentary secretary made reference to a number of cases, some of which received a lot of attention in the press. Because Canadian citizens were pursuing their claims in the courts, there was some interest in how the courts would interpret the right of the litigant to bring the action and the right of the successful plaintiff to realize on the judgment received in the Canadian courts against the property of a foreign country.
I can understand the interest of the government to bring forward this kind of legislation. There is a manifestation around the world of a greater growth of so-called centrally controlled economies where the state is involved directly in trading and business opportunities not only within their own borders but in other countries.
The question arises by virtue of the fact that they are foreign governments and why should the immunity which is

June 23, 1981
State Immunity Act
afforded diplomatic representatives in Canada be extended to those people involved in commercial activities in this country. I think any rational person and people involved from other countries fully understand that if they are involved in commercial activities they should operate according to the rules of the place in which the business is carried on. That is understood in commercial terms and I think it is understood in diplomatic terms.
Having looked at this bill from that point of view, I think it deals with the whole question of establishing, codifying or declaring that Canadian citizens do have the right to bring an * action against foreign governments or their agencies carrying on commercial activity.
The next step, of course, will be to look at the question whether a judgment can be executed once a Canadian citizen plaintiff does obtain a judgment in Canada against a foreign state. The parliamentary secretary will understand that it is one thing to get a judgment but quite another altogether to collect as a result of that judgment against any litigant, let alone a foreign state.
There are other questions which arise regarding this particular bill. I do not propose to spend a lot of time discussing the bill itself at this stage, but it is our view that this bill should be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for at least one sitting in order to obtain answers to some more or less legalistic questions that arise about things that have occurred, to me at least, and will occur I am sure to members of that committee, regarding its operation, even though the matter has been discussed before the Senate committee which has had the opportunity of doing quite a bit of work on it, obtaining some very excellent evidence by departmental officials, Mr. Strayer, and Professor Castel of Osgoode Hall of the University of Toronto.
In any event, I want to deal briefly with some aspects of the bill and raise a couple of questions which might be dealt with at the committee. I want to make absolutely certain that in passing this legislation we are getting ourselves in the best possible situation as far as Canadian citizens are concerned to realize on judgments, and that is the area I would like to have investigated by the committee.
Secondly, in passing this legislation I want to be satisfied that the whole matter of constitutional propriety is being observed and we are not getting ourselves into a hornet's nest with regard to jurisdictional questions when we ask the courts to set certain guidelines and rules in relation to the service process against foreign states. I will deal with those matters briefly in the course of my remarks in a few minutes.
In terms of this particular legislation, the principle underlying this bill is one of trade-off. Certainly Canadians want a right of action and also the ability to execute judgments against commercial activity carried on by foreign states. We all appreciate and fully understand and support the concept referred to by the parliamentary secretary, that is the pragmatic necessity, quite apart from the divine rule of kings and all those other historical considerations referred to in his introductory remarks, of foreign states having immunity for
diplomatic representatives carrying out their duties in a foreign country. I do not think there is any question about that. The question is whether these interests can be balanced in legislation.
As I understand it, the current situation is that where there is a dispute or a matter that may lead to litigation, our external affairs department very often steps in and uses that very good office to mediate or negotiate between a foreign state and the litigant in Canada. Officials spend a lot of time very effectively in settling a good number of cases between litigants and foreign states carrying on commercial activities. This is an ongoing process and I understand from the record they have done very well in this regard.
Now we are to have a stature that will attempt to state or clarify better the situation with regard to the rights of litigants in this country. Reference has been made by the parliamentary secretary to the fact that this is a codification of the present law. I think it fair to say that the courts in Canada, particularly in Quebec and Ontario, have been moving through the process of judicial precedent toward the application of the concept of limited immunity in commercial activities. They have in fact applied in their judgments the restrictive theory, granting immunity only to the degree necessary for the free conduct of international relations by a foreign state. The matter has not really come as such before the Supreme Court of Canada, except indirectly, so there has not been a specific judgment on the law as it now stands by this high court of the land. That court is probably preoccupied with other things these days. There are a couple of items before it which I am sure are occupying some time.
The fact of the matter is that in the case of Venne v. The Democratic Republic of Congo, Chief Justice Laskin in his judgment indicated approval of the concept of limited or restricted immunity. It becomes clear to me from that particular judgment that Chief Justice Laskin would be inclined to approve of the state of the law and the judgments which have been brought forward in the lower courts that in fact recognize restricted immunity.
The aim of the bill is to establish a statutory guide for the courts in relation to actions against foreign states brought before them. If one looks at the impact of this particular legislation, one could say that conceivably there will be an expansion of jurisdiction in the courts as the bill does in fact clearly state that there is declared henceforth, on the passage of the bill, a restriction on a foreign state's immunity.
As I mentioned before, one of the results of this bill will be that the rules of the courts of the provinces will have to be modified to reflect the procedural provisions of the act. I simply raise this point because I would like to get some clarification from departmental officials, the minister or his parliamentary secretary on that aspect.
There may be a constitutional problem involved regarding the provisions of the bill in relation to service, deemed service and so on, which heretofore have been matters regarding provincial rules of court across the country. I know the evidence is that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) did in fact
June 23, 1981

communicate with the attorneys general across Canada and received no particular objection to the legislation. On the other hand, he received no response from some provinces. It seems to me we should be clear in our own minds before passing this legislation that we are not going to get into a mixed up situation in provincial jurisdiction on the procedural side of the bill.
The other aspect I just want to canvass a little more thoroughly in committee deals with the definition of "commercial activity". I understand the evidence which was given and the reasons for the provisions of the bill relating to commercial activity and the definition of that term.
As the parliamentary secretary has pointed out, commercial activity is not defined in any particularized way in the legislation. Basically, as it says in the act, it is any transaction or act that by reason of its nature is commercial activity. In other words, commercial activity is commercial activity. So it is going to be left to the courts on a case by case consideration of the individual circumstances to develop the jurisprudence and a definition of commercial activity in that way.
The parliamentary secretary has made reference to the fact that this is based on the U.S. approach as opposed to that of the United Kingdom. There are some aspects of this bill which may well have some basis in pragmatic consideration, as I said, or legal justification as to why the bill contains certain exclusions with respect to its operation. However, as Professor Castel said in the course of his testimony, one of the most important things that can be done under this bill is to define how a Canadian citizen can go about getting paid. He said the bill should try to clarify the right of a citizen to relief, a right to which he is entitled. It is one thing, as I said at the outset, to specify that a citizen has a right to bring an action and obtain a judgment, but that is only part of the whole process. The really important question is: once you have judgment, can you collect? That is where I think the bill requires further consideration.
By way of example let me refer to the discussions about collecting rent for embassy premises. Ottawa landlords will all perk up their ears at that suggestion. There are only two people watching this particular debate right now; the representative of the embassy landlords association, and the Ottawa chief of police who is wondering whether there is anything in this bill which will allow him to collect all the parking tickets they have been unable to collect because of diplomatic immunity. The parliamentary secretary is watching too-I should not count him out.
In a situation where embassy premises are damaged, the question arises as to whether or not the Canadian landlord can collect. Certainly he has a cause of action, but under the provisions of clause 11 unless the property is used for commercial purposes, it is exempt from execution of judgment. There are other examples. Clause 10, I believe, specifically deals with the remedies one has against a foreign state. It does not include specific performance, injunctions or an order for the recovery of land unless the foreign state consents. I have no particular objection to the idea of codifying the law if it makes it easier for average citizens to understand and pursue their rights, because I am in favour of the concept of restricted immunity and the enhancement of the rights of Canadians with respect to foreign commercial activities in Canada. Somewhere near the bottom of that list, one would come up with an item on the necessity to re-examine the length of the writ period. It would be somewhere near the bottom of that list. The fact of the matter is that since the last amendment to the Elections Act in 1974, a committee, chaired by the Chief Electoral Officer, involving elected members from each of the parties in the House and involving representatives of the political organizations of each of the parties, has been meeting on a regular basis and discussing the Elections Act, examining it in detail and recommending changes to this act. I am aware of it because some four years ago I participated in that committee for about a year and a half. The committee produced a long list of desirable changes to the Elections Act. Any responsible government that felt that it might now be appropriate to reform, review, alter or update the Elections Act would start with the committee's recommendations. The committee worked on this matter for at least five years. It has gone over the list with a fine tooth comb, and has brought in an enormous list of recommendations. If these are not included in the proposed changes, then what was the purpose of the committee? When the government decided to change the Elections Act, why did it pursue this little change-the reduction of the campaign period to 47 days from 60 days?
I would like to see many kinds of changes to the Elections Act. For example, the act that we have been operating under since 1974 restricts election expenses. I think most people agree with that, but the levels established in the act are now, because of the uncontrolled inflation which the government will not address, no longer applicable.

A similar document was produced by my association recently at a cost of $3,500. Office space in downtown Calgary, which I represent, costs at least three times as much today as in 1974 when these figures were first produced. The cost of radio and television advertising for an election is now beyond the reach of a constituency campaign, given the umbrella figures that were appropriate in 1974.

The redistribution formula is something that must be changed, Mr. Speaker. It was put in place as a kind of compromise after the delay of the redistribution that was supposed to occur in 1973. At that time we had three rather senior members of the House, the late member for Prince Albert, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who all had reason to be concerned because in their respective provinces they would lose a seat. Being three very influential members of Parliament, they succeeded in having the redistribution delayed until after the 1974 election, at which time a new redistribution formula was introduced which catered to the Liberal party, in the sense of looking after the interests of the province from which the majority of its seats came.
There was great objection to that formula at the time, so there was a semi-compromise. It was allowed that after the first election when the formula was in place, there would be an opportunity to review the consequences of the redistribution formula and recommend change. Unfortunately, we then had a series of very quick elections and the committee reference to which the act refers fell between the cracks and nothing happened. That redistribution formula, however, after the census which is now taking place, would have the result of bringing an additional 30 or more members to this House. That is a change which will do nothing but damage this institution and damage the national government further in terms of its ability to represent the public. There is already such an incredible level of frustration in this institution, on both sides of the House because of the inability of the ordinary member to be heard, to ask questions or make speeches, that the addition of 30 new members will only compound the problem.
It would not be a bad thing for the executive, of course. If you are the king, it does not hurt to have a large Parliament. Any student of politics or sociology recognizes that it is much easier to control a large committee than a small committee and that a House of 300 members is easier for a government to manipulate than a House of 200. Of course, a House of 400 would be easier still to manipulate. It is easy to see the reasoning behind the desire for growth in the size of the institution.
If one is genuinely concerned about the people represented by the members of this House, or is generally interested in this House of Commons and wants to see it function as a real Parliament with real legislative ability and authority, then the last thing that one would be pursuing would be an increase in the number of members.
There are also inequities in that redistribution formula in the way seats are distributed as between provinces. I hate to impute motives to the draftsmen of that redistribution formula one of whom was the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). By coincidence the result is a redistribution formula which means the largest populated ridings in the country are Alberta and British Columbia which, by coincidence, are the two areas where there are no Liberal members. It is a coincidence I am sure, and if you believe that, you believe the world is flat. It is no coincidence at all.
If you also believed that there are serious questions in terms of western alienation, and if you also believed, as any sane Canadian must believe, that there are serious people in western Canada who are considering separation because they feel so detached from this institution in terms of its ability to represent them, then you would not allow that inequity to continue on the books. Any government that really believed, not in a rhetorical but a real sense, that national unity was important and that it is important for the regions of this country to feel a part of the whole, would be addressing that inequity of the redistribution formula. The government would

be addressing it now to ensure that there is not more fodder or more ammunition for West-Fed, western concepts, western Canada parties and the other groups springing into being daily to represent that frustration which exists out there.
There is a great need for change in the electoral system in this country through the Canada Elections Act. A committee has been meeting for years on a regular basis every two or three weeks with a long list of reforms on its agenda. In other words, the whole fence needs mending. But the government at this time of record inflation, record interest and mortgage rates and high unemployment brings in a bill to fix one fence post, a bill to reduce the election period from 60 days to 47 days. Why is the government doing that? Given this broad array of necessary reforms, why is the government bringing in this bill at this time? I think the answer is not that difficult to deduce. What the government wants is a quick campaign, the quicker the campaign the better. A quick campaign serves the interests of the incumbent.
In this country we have a system where the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) alone can decide the election date. He can decide when the House is to be dissolved and an election called. With the very sophisticated polling techniques that are available and primed daily with a minister for propaganda who sends out contracts on a weekly basis to keep the machinery in order, it is very easy for the Prime Minister to have very up-to-date assessments of public opinion. Therefore, he can have a very accurate assessment of how his party would do if an election were held immediately. Clearly if it were in his power to dissolve this House and have an election tomorrow it would be impossible to ever have a change of government. It would be impossible for any change to be made, given that ability to conduct polls to find out what the people are thinking. By calling an election immediately, that would be it.
Obviously, if an election were held six months after the Prime Minister called it, the election period would not make any difference because people's views change during that time. The shorter an election period, the greater the advantage to the incumbent. So it is very easy to see why we have this bill coming in from the government now. The government has no intention of making the other changes in the Canada Elections Act. The government has no intention of changing the redistribution formula. What we will get are pious speeches from the Prime Minister saying, "Now that I have the Constitution home, I will try to make the regions of the country feel that they are part of the whole", and all of that poppycock coming forth.
But we will not have any of those changes if the powers that be in the PMO and in the Liberal party are able to get this bill through. This bill gives them an advantage over what we have now. Who knows, there may be a change in leadership of the governing party before the next election. Would it not be great to have a leadership convention, with the accompanying deification of the winner, no matter who it is-some reporter digs up a former school teacher who says "I saw greatness when he was four years old" and all of that kind of nonsense-followed immediately by a very short election period, and you would
Canada Elections Act
never have to go through the nonsense of having perhaps some other party forming the government or winning a seat or two!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
I am sure the government would love to do away with elections altogether. We can hear members opposite say "That might be a little tough, but we will work at it gradually." I hear one of the sheep baaing. We know you can talk. If you can demonstrate you can think, you will really be accomplishing something.
We have a limitation in the Canada Elections Act. It concerns the advertising period which is limited to the last 29 days of the election campaign. To the public, the only real involvement with the election is the last 29 days. The ads interrupt the soap operas, and sometimes the free time political broadcasts cut out Laverne and Shirley and other such cultural programs. But whether an election campaign consists of 47 days, 60 days or 75 days does not affect the Canadian public-it affects us. We partisans are out there pounding on doors, handing out literature, shaking hands and doing all those kinds of things, but the voting public is not affected. They do not know an election is going on until the last 29 days when the formal advertising period occurs.
Reducing the time of an election campaign from 60 days to 47 days does not save the public the pain of an election period. It does not affect the public at all. Perhaps we ourselves save shoe leather. I am glad to admit that I am an incumbent. Frankly, the 47-day period appeals to me in that sense. I say make it two weeks or even a week, and I will never be defeated. I am an incumbent. The shorter the period, the better. If you are really looking at the democratic system, if you are really concerned and you really think the ability to change a member of Parliament from time to time and the ability to change governments from time to time is an important part of democracy, then you do not sit back so complacently and so easily and say "sure, you want a shorter election period, then we will give it to you" because we are all incumbents. It is very nice for us to cut off our opponents at the pass.
We desperately need to reform the way this country functions. Unfortunately, this institution and its members of Parliament do not reflect this country. The national government here is not a national government to far too many Canadians. Ottawa is almost an adversary, a corporate body which is not the people's in any real sense. People from my region do not look upon this government as being their first government. Their first government is in Edmonton. I think that is sad and it bothers me. But that cannot be changed through some powerplay via energy programs, nationalizing of the oil industry, putting in Crown corporations or forcing a Constitution through. The way to change it is to let the people really have some influence here in the national government.

June 23, 1981
Canada Elections Act
This bill is just another cute little game to give more advantage to the governing party. If the government is really interested in democracy and wants to make people feel they are Canadians, it should not be looking at these kinds of changes. I could suggest a lot of changes, but I know they would all be resisted by the PMO and the Prime Minister because human nature does not voluntarily give up power. Nobody does.
Since all the power rests with those opposite, we get into a Catch-22 situation. They have too much power for anyone to force them to give up any. No one voluntarily gives up power, so we are caught in a Catch-22 situation. We should seriously examine the possibility of fixed election dates in this country where an election is held four or five years after the previous election, unless a government is defeated by a vote of confidence.
That would be a tremendous change in the system and a tremendous reduction in prime ministerial power. It would not reduce the power of the House of Commons or the national government, only the power of one person in this country.
We need changes in the way this place operates. Canadians decry, and we do as well, the party system that requires its members to vote as a block. Many of us say privately, albeit not publicly, that we wish there was some way that members could vote according to their conscience without being mavericks. With the present voting system, the Speaker asks, "All those in favour". The Prime Minister or the Leader of the Opposition is the first to stand, followed by members of his party, row by row. The system is designed to focus attention on anyone who dares to be a maverick and take a position different from that of his leader. That is the deliberate effect. I think it should be changed.
Lately there have been a lot of editorials and columns by writers too lazy to look at the real problems of the day about the question of MPs salaries. About a year ago I saw a column in The Globe and Mail by Geoffrey Stevens who had an idea which I wonder why we cannot discuss some time. That is an examination of the differential in salaries between members and ministers. The Americans have a philosophy which says that in a democracy the most important people are the general public and the next most important are those elected by the general public. Their system states that no one shall be paid more than an elected official because he represents the people, and in a democracy no one is more important. Anybody who is appointed, therefore, must be of lesser importance in their government. If you believe in a democracy and in the people electing members, then the most important person should be the member, the person elected. Anybody appointed should be lesser.
Under the American system, no one who is appointed can get a higher salary than a congressman or senator. I wonder what would happen in our system if we had uniform salaries in this institution with cabinet ministers getting no more and no less than the other members of Parliament.
Mir. Nielsen: Gerry would be back in Nova Scotia.
Mir. Andre: A couple of things would happen. First, it would be much easier for the prime minister to change cabinets. He would not be penalizing someone he dropped from the cabinet or rewarding someone he left in.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
There is no rational reason for bringing forward this bill to reduce the election period from 60 to 47 days except for the desire to give the incumbent that little extra edge which comes from a shorter election period. There are many reforms needed, including changes to the elections act. The list which the Chief Electoral Officer has is enormous.
The danger in giving quick passage to this bill is that we will never see the other reforms. If the government House leader was sincere in his earlier statements and indications about electoral reform and if the government would like to see those changes, my party would be ready and willing to participate in any form of committee, task force, what have you, to see whether we could reach an accord on the appropriate changes to make from the enormous list which the Chief Electoral Officer has. We would be prepared to work together as members of Parliament, not as adversaries but as members interested in the electoral process. The government should assemble the appropriate legislation and bring it forward. It could be given very speedy passage through this House of Commons. We would have a better election act to guide us in terms of the next election, whenever it might come. In the meantime, we on this side feel that the problems of this country are not the fact that elections are run for 60 rather than 47 days. There is no great clamour from the public to reduce the election period. I have not received a single letter or phone call about it and I would be surprised if anyone in this House has.
June 23, 1981

Frankly, it is baffling and embarrassing to be here-representing my constituents who are wondering how they can afford the 18 per cent mortgage they have to renew-debating a bill which is absurd in terms of the needs of the nation and equally absurd in terms of the electoral process.
The priorities of this government are beyond belief. The opposition does not have any authority, and maybe we should look at reforms in this regard, to bring in legislative programs to deal with the problems of the day. Perhaps we should look at a reform to allow the opposition in a situation like this to address the priorities of the country where the government refuses to do so. Perhaps that is the kind of reform we need and should be examining.
We are forced to debate the government's agenda. This afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) suggested we adjourn for this evening if the government had nothing to discuss so that the Quebec members could enjoy the celebrations on the eve of St. Jean Baptiste Day. That would be serving the country a lot better than sitting here discussing this bill which does not benefit the country one whit. It benefits our democratic process not one whit. It addresses the priorities, even on elections, not one whit. What does it do? It gives the incumbent some advantage, and therefore it is worth pursuing, at least in their priorities. I am sorry, it may be hot and humid in Ottawa; it may be getting to be the silly season, but it is not so silly that they are going to pull a fast one like that on this House. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to be either as long or as profound as the previous speaker. I must say that generally I find myself in agreement with the provisions of the bill we have before us. My objection to it would be that it does not contain those other things, some of which were referred to earlier by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), that should be included in a bill to make all manner of amendments to the Elections Act.
I am in favour of the reduction in the period of the writ from 60 days to 47 days, and the main reason is that this is what I feel is the wish of the people, at least in my constituency. We have in this day and age virtual saturation coverage in election campaigns on the radio, television and in the newspapers. People get heartily sick and tired of listening to all this. Every time they switch the television set on there is the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or some candidate running for office.
Most members of the public have either made up their minds who or which party they intend to vote for before the writ is even issued, or they tend to wait until election day or a few days before to make up their minds. As long as you take it in reasonable terms, it does not really matter whether it is 30 days or 80 days. Many countries have an election period of only 30 days, and various provinces in Canada have only 30 days. So honestly I do not think it would have that big a bearing on the result of the election. I would support this
Canada Elections Act
measure because I feel this is what the public of Canada, particularly people in my constituency, would favour.
A number of people would argue that in large constituencies such as my own it is very difficult for members or candidates to travel to every community, but in the days of jet aircraft it is really not that difficult. It might be difficult to get to every little community with 20, 30 or 40 people, but it is not difficult to get to the vast majority of communities containing 85 per cent of the population.
It must be remembered that the situation is the same for every candidate. Every candidate has to figure out how he must use his time to what he considers his maximum advantage. No one person really has an advantage over the other. I guess the 60-day period goes back to the days of the horse and buggy, the days when it was necessary for the party leaders to travel from one end of Canada to the other and back perhaps several times by train. That does not happen anymore. We have instant communication with radio, TV and the wire services, so that a speech made in Halifax is reported the same day in Vancouver. There have been developments in printing technology that enable the Chief Electoral Officer to do his job fairly quickly. This also enables candidates to get their literature and posters printed fairly rapidly. I do not really think a reduction from the present 60 days to the proposed 47 days puts too much disadvantage in anyone's way.
It has been argued that a reduced writ period would favour the incumbents, both the incumbent member and the incumbent party which at present forms the government. If the period were reduced to a week, as suggested earlier this evening, that might indeed be the case. But with a writ period still in excess of that commonly used in most provinces and many other countries in the world, I do not think that is really the case. Any assistance it might give to an incumbent, either the individual or party, would be fairly marginal at best.
I can think of circumstances in which the very opposite might be the case. When a government chooses the time it wants to go back to the people, the advantage might be with a shorter election period. If we take as an example the opposite, as happened early in 1980, I think a longer election period would have worked to the advantage of the incumbent government. That election was the 18-cent election, and if the people had had more time to really look into the promises being made by what at that time was the opposition party, they would have realized what nonsense those promises were. They would have realized that the price of energy had to go up, so at that time a longer period would have worked to the advantage of the incumbent, which was the Conservative party. As long as changes are made within reason, any advantages or disadvantages are going to be pretty marginal. The public of Canada would be well served by not having to listen to and look at us and other candidates during election campaigns for the time they have to at present.
There are a number of areas in which the bill is remiss. There are a number of areas the bill does not cover. These were listed on several occasions during the earlier debate on

June 23, 1981
Canada Elections Act
this bill. I want to repeat one or two and maybe add a few, some of specific local interest.
One of the most important things not addressed by the bill is the ever-expanding membership of this House. The present number is 282, and I understand that if an election were to be held today, or within a short period of time, the number of members re-elected would be some 312. This number would escalate exponentially as the population of Canada increases. I do not think we should adopt the British system where they have 650 or so MPs. I always wonder what all those 650 people do.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: We wonder what all these do.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
That is true too, especially those over there. I wonder what they do all the time and I have never yet been able to figure it out. I think probably we have too many members in this House now. Rather than an increase to 312 I would like to see a decrease to 250. Let us try that. The more members you have, the more the part played by an individual member is reduced. He finds himself relegated to being a number, to just standing up when a vote is called. If there was an equal allocation of the time of this House to members, and you took the number of minutes in a day that we sit on average and divide it by the number of members, it would come out to about one minute per day. Of course, the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and front bench members on both sides have, together with the Speaker, a disproportionate amount of that time, and rightfully so, there is no objection to that, but it leaves the average member of this House with something much less than a minute, or five minutes a week. If you give one 20-minute speech a month, you have used up your time. I think by expanding the number of members, you take away from the individual member and you relegate him to the position of one small cog in the wheel. At the same time you are increasing the influence of the executive and increasing the power of the Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues.
We on this side of the House, and many members on the other side, have said that we desire a system whereby the ordinary member of the House would play a much greater part. That, sir, is my speech from the back row. Ten years from now, when I am in the front row, I might change my mind slightly.
I guess one of the main problems we have to face if we are to maintain or, hopefully, reduce the number of members, is the fact that certain provinces where the population has not been expanding at all will find themselves in a position where they would lose members. If I understand it correctly, the reason the rapid expansion was adopted the last time around was that no province wanted to lose members. That problem has to be addressed, and I am sure it is within our capabilities to solve it.
I would like now to extend some compliments to the Chief Electoral Officer of Canada, Jean-Marc Hamel. I was one of the members who took advantage of section 59(2) of the
elections act after the last election and sent him correspondence with a number of views on how the election had been run and what could be done to improve the procedures, particularly in my constituency. I was most pleased with his response, his attentiveness and the way in which he dealt with my letter. He obviously gave the matter the attention that I at least thought it deserved. Most of the points I brought to his attention were technical matters and I do not wish to go into them in any detail right now. He assured me that he already knew about a lot of these technical matters and they were on the way to being cleared up. However, I have one or two comments to make about ways in which the election process might be made a little more effective. These should be, but are not, in the bill before us tonight and I would hope to see some of these matters dealt with during the term of this Parliament.
The first one deals with the appointment of returning officers. The system we now have goes back many years. The job of returning officer is handed out by the party in power; it is a patronage position. I do not think that is right. I think the choice of returning officer in each riding should be left to the Chief Electoral Officer of Canada. The returning officer should be directly responsible and answerable to him, and the appointment should not be made with patronage in mind.
The system we now have is really a nineteenth century system and I would hope we have progressed in this respect as we have done with many other public officials. These positions should not be handed out on a platter with the idea of some political return; rather, they should be filled by people who are technically the most proficient and able to carry on the work.
If that were to happen, the number of complaints levied against returning officers and their deputies would be much reduced. Election personnel are nominated by the party in power, and the people not of that party always have the suspicion that something might possibly go wrong. There is always the suspicion that the election officer might in some small way be going out of his way to help the representative of the party that appointed him. I would hope that could be changed. Perhaps it is not even necessary to change the legislation, just the practice.
The second point I would like to bring to the attention of this House is rather a parochial one, but it deals with section 61.2(1) of the elections act. This section allows for special publication and broadcast rules for the territories, those areas of Canada which unfortunately are not yet provinces. The idea behind this is quite reasonable. In the days when there were no real radio or TV stations in the north, when it took a long time for newspapers to circulate, when in fact there were not really that many newspapers, it was perhaps necessary. The first day you are allowed to advertise in the press or over electronic media is the twenty-ninth day before the election, and that restriction does not apply to the Territories. I think we have progressed sufficiently in northern Canada that we are now not much different from the rest of the country. There is no real need for this provision any more. It is difficult because if you go to a newspaper or radio station prior to the twenty-ninth day to place an advertisement, they have all had a notice
June 23, 1981

circulated to them from the Chief Electoral Officer saying that this is prohibited. They are not aware of this little technicality in the bill which says that does not apply to the territories. If you do get something on the radio, somebody will pick it up down in Alberta and there will be all kinds of complaints because this guy is advertising before he should be. They are not aware of the exemption. There was so much difficulty with this provision in the last federal election in the Northwest Territories, that to the best of my knowledge none of the candidates took advantage of it. That, I think, is a good indication that the provision has outlived its usefulness.
My third point is with regard to aid to illiterate persons, and also persons who do not read the orthography used for printing in English or French; rather they use the syllabic method in which the Inuktitut language is commonly printed. This matter, at least the syllabic part of it, is of more interest to my colleague, the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar), who unfortunately is not here this evening.
There are many people in his constituency who do not read the normal orthography used in the rest of Canada; they use the syllabic system. Consequently, they are unable to read the names of the various candidates. It would be a fairly simple matter to allow, by some rule or regulation under the elections act, the names also to be printed in syllabics. It is no great difficulty at all, it is just a technicality. I hope that can be done.
My next point is on the use of photographs either on the ballot papers or on the walls of polling stations to aid people who are not able to read or write. There are many of these people in my constituency. This has been the subject of great local debate. I am referring not only to federal elections, but to territorial and municipal elections as well. That problem has been solved for all elections other than federal ones.
The various band councils first suggested the idea of putting the photographs of candidates on the ballot papers. It proved to be very successful, and the municipal ordinance was amended to allow that practice to be followed in municipal elections. It is quite a common practice in many communities in my constituency. There were some technical difficulties respecting the use of photographs on the actual ballot paper in territorial elections, but with the assistance of the Chief Electoral Officer acting as adviser to the territorial legislature, a system was adopted whereby the photographs of candidates could be displayed in polling stations with their names underneath. Thus people were able to memorize the name for the limited period of time it took them to go into the booths and mark the ballots.
There is great difficulty in this regard. People will come up to us on the street and say, "I would like to vote either for you or your opponent, but there is no way I can read the names. Could you tell me where your name appears on the ballot paper? Is it first, second or third?" If the candidate is number two, he or she is very lucky; it does not matter which way up they have the ballot paper because they will mark it in the
Canada Elections Act
right place. But, if the candidate is number one and they have the ballot paper upside down, he or she is out of luck. Certain exceptions to the general rule could be made for areas where there are large numbers of people who are unable to read or write. It has been demonstrated that it is possible. It is just a matter of putting our minds to it.
That is as far as I want to go. I could pursue this matter for a long time by repeating many of the arguments and by indicating the omissions of other speakers, but I do not really want to do that at this time. I have pointed out the most important general omissions and also some of the rather specific ones. In conclusion, I support the provisions of Bill C-58 which is before us, but I would certainly like to see it expanded to address some of the other unresolved problems.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on this bill, particularly with respect to the comments of the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre). It seems the growing tendency in the House is to talk out a bill basically because it does not go far enough. If we were acting co-operatively in the House, we would realize the difficulties facing governments in power. Unfortunately, perhaps for the opposition but not for the country, the Conservatives were not in power long enough to come to grips with the fact that we cannot have everything we want at any given stage. When we have a relatively simple bill which has a positive effect, I find it difficult to understand why it is being opposed, yet I see this happening all over.
The hon. members of the NDP opposed Bill C-48, the oil and gas bill, because for some reason or other it did not go far enough. But there is probably no combination of hon. members in the House who could bring in a better or tougher bill. They are opposing bills because they do not get exactly what they want, therefore we do not get anything and too much time is spent talking these things out.
This is a good bill which does a very small but positive thing. As I travelled around the country during election time, particularly in my constituency, there is no doubt people told me that elections were too long. Of course they used some other words to express themselves, but they just did not believe that elections needed to be so long. I think this is a positive bill. 1 would like to see it go further. I would like to see a permanent list. I would like to see us reduce the time to 30 days or 35 days, which would be an adequate amount of time to run an intelligent election in any country.
We must remember that any election starts years before it is actually called. We are in elections all the time. We are debating where we are going and where the next government will go. It is never sudden. Although the last election was very sudden in one respect, it was a continuation of the debate which had been ongoing in the House for several years.
Basically we have a decent and good Elections Act. It is better than it was years ago. It does many good things. As the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) just indicated, we still need some changes. I do not fault him on that. I

June 23, 1981
Canada Elections Act
think he made an honest effort to point out some of the things he wanted.
This is a good bill because it eliminates some of the abuses, for instance, in the province of Ontario where there is no limit on the amount of money a candidate can spend. With the kind of devices available to candidates and the money which can be spent on television and so on, it is almost possible to get anyone elected if there is no limit and one has enough money. One very positive provision of the act eliminated this by indicating that the amount of money a candidate could spend would be based upon the number of people in his or her constituency. I think it is a reasonable limit. For example, in my area the limit is approximately $26,000 per candidate. This provision makes a lot of sense.
Certainly there are other positive provisions in the act which tend to make elections a very orderly process, something that makes people believe there is a degree of honesty on the part of all concerned. But there is something seriously missing.
Before coming to the House, I spent 22 years as an educator, a high school principal and so on. I have seen young people growing up and spending ten years to 12 years on the average in school; of course a lot of them spend many more years than that. I remember on one occasion I went into a classroom to discuss a given subject with some young people. They spent some time trying to understand. There was a certain amount of teaching going on and there were questions back and forth. Certain information was being passed back and forth between teacher and pupil. Then I was put in an opposite situation when I became involved in the political scene, and I was confounded by the fact that I had to express myself in terms of the press and in terms of an election in 30-second jingles. There is no possible way that one can convey intelligent ideas in 30-second jingles. One reason most people say that the elections are too long is that they have heard the same jingles for 21, 26 or 28 days, as is the case in federal elections, and they have heard nothing else. There is no decent communication. Many of the candidates are chosen because of their ability to deal with the jingle. In many cases candidates are not chosen because they have good minds, or because they are thoughtful and have been looking at the situation for a long time. Very often there are other reasons why they have been chosen. Someone props them up and they run through an election.
I am told that one candidate in my area had six professional organizers working through an election campaign. They just walked around and told the candidate the right things to do. It was all managed. There is no way I can appear on television, unless I blow the whole $26,000 for 15 or 20 minutes, to take part in an intelligent debate where the issues are seriously dealt with.
Let us say that an election was held today and we had to deal with monetarism versus low interest rates. That is an important subject to Canadian people, yet it would be virtually impossible to discuss that issue in an election campaign
because we have never managed to take the matter seriously. We have let the media take the situation over. We have said to the Canadian public who have been in schools for ten to 15 years, who are used to communication, "You do not deserve that. All you are worth is a jingle."
If democracy is to survive in this country, we must do something better than what we are doing. We must make sure that candidates who run in elections are able to express themselves as intelligent human beings in terms of the issues which pertain to the election. People say that they do not know where we stand after an election. How can I convey serious notions about monetarism, interest rates or federal fiscal arrangements in a 30-second jingle? I cannot do it. It is not possible. It seems to me we should be putting our time and energy into finding out how it is possible to have decent debate, debate that will involve people.
I hate to say this after nine years as a politician, but I do not feel that the public sees me as being very important, as being very relevant. I am not just talking about myself but about politicians in general. They see us in some kind of dirty way. They think we need all these rules, otherwise we would cheat. I feel a great deal of this is caused by the way we present ourselves, with the electoral laws which we have which permit us to be sold by jingle, something which contains all kinds of words but no real substance. It is no wonder the public sees us as not being worth $30,000, or $32,000 a year, or whatever our take-home pay is.
Somewhere along the line before I leave this place I hope to establish an image for myself which is a cut above what I have just outlined. I would like to see all politicians being able to talk seriously to the public about issues. I do not want to do it in a 30-second or 60-second jingle.
I feel this bill is something worthwhile. I hope other members share my views on this matter. We should really get down to running elections seriously in an intelligent way so that the people of Canada can become involved in what is going on and can try to make sure that their candidates understand what is happening.

Mr. Speaker, I will speak to the bill. The hon. member spoke about this, and surely members opposite will

give me the opportunity to retaliate. What kind of one-sided outfit is this becoming?
The government is trying to give the impression that it is doing something for the Canadian people through this bill, Bill C-58. Imagine cutting 13 days off the election time. What saving will that mean to the Canadian taxpayer? I would like one hon. member opposite to stand up and tell me what benefit there will be to the Canadian taxpayers as a result of cutting 13 days off the Canadian election. It riles me to think that this government lacks the imagination to take advantage of so many opportunities to do something for the Canadian people.
If you will permit me, Mr. Speaker, I will list several of those points. First and foremost is the bill which I presented in this House of Commons. I trust that it will be debated some time in the not too distant future. I hope that there will be a limitation on the membership of this House. I recognize that other members have already referred to this point; but if there is one thing we politicians must do, it is to realize that the taxpayer cannot continue to accept the excessive load which is being placed on their backs by the political system. My friend, the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) referred to the number of members in the House of Commons in Great Britain. I recognize that there are 635 members in that House. It must also be recognized that there are 60 million people living in Great Britain. We have provincial legislatures which also serve the 25 million people who live in Canada. We must not forget that. If the government wanted to bring in a worthwhile measure at this time, why does it not bring in a bill which will freeze the membership of the House of Commons until such time as it can be substantiated that there should be an increase in our membership?
I must ask what the priority of this government is. It brings before us a bill which will limit the election period by 13 days. There are so many opportunities which can be taken advantage of through the Elections Act. What about the swearing-in ceremonies for a great many of the people in our urban centres within that period of time?
The hon. member who had the floor before me mentioned that people get awfully tired of jingles. This bill will not change that at all. There will still be 28 days of advertising, which is another area with which I certainly do not agree. I do not think the government should be infringing on the rights of Canadians the way it is through the advertising which takes place through the campaigns. Editorial writers are frightened to comment because those comments may be construed as advertising. People are afraid to put anything on paper prior to that 28 days for fear of being charged. We recognize that there have been infringements of this regulation. I do not really see why that is so very important.
I would like to debate those kinds of issues rather than the matter of just cutting back the election period by 13 days. I know that people get tired of elections. People get tired of politicians. They get too much of it, simply because there has not been enough production from the system. We on this side
Canada Elections Act
of the House cannot do anything about it if the government does not provide the leadership and the imagination which is required. It is up to the government. Surely, the Canadian people must recognize the void which must exist in the minds of the government members in order for them to bring a bill like this forward at this time.
What about the people who are disenfranchised simply because there is no provision in some of the smaller rural centres for swearing in? Surely, those areas should be allowed to have that type of privilege which is granted to urban centres. What about those people who are disenfranchised because they are hospitalized? We are not doing anything about that, unless the government decides that it will change some of the regulations guiding the Chief Electoral Officer. Those are changes which would be of benefit to the Canadian people. Why are we not talking about that? The government does not say anything about that at all. No mention is made about that in the bill.
What about the handicapped? What is the government doing about making the polls accessible to those people too? What about the areas in large rural ridings where regulations make people drive 20, 30 or 40 miles to exercise their franchise? What are we doing about that?
What are we doing about the dictatorial attitude of the commissioners who set up the boundary lines? What consideration is given to that? None at all. There is nothing in this bill which would do something for that. What are we doing about the boundary lines coinciding with county lines within the rural areas? Nothing at all. What are we doing about the boundary lines coinciding with the social habits of people, their lines of communication and their travelling habits? Nothing at all.
There are so many areas in which we could be doing something for these people. Therefore, I have to severely criticize the government at this time for bringing in a bill which just limits the election period for 13 days. Does Your Honour know what will happen? The people who are involved in that election will start campaigning earlier, that is all. They will have their house in order, they will have their machinery geared up and ready to run, and that is all. It will not change anything. There is nothing in this bill which will change anything. There is nothing in this bill which will change the advertising regulations. Therefore, the people will still be subjected, whether it be good or bad, to 28 days of advertising.
One of the reasons this session of Parliament has been devoid of any constructive suggestion is that the government is apparently devoid of the ability to bring anything forward that is imaginative. Therefore members, especially those on the government side, should really take a look at these matters to see what we can do to improve the reputation of the House of Commons. Certainly I must emphasize this once again. Increasing the membership of the House of Commons is not the answer to our problem. I realize that is outside the purview of this bill, but we have to seize these opportunities when they
