Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me the opportunity to make some remarks on Bill C-58, to amend the Canada Elections Act. Before I commence my address, let me comment briefly on the remarks
Canada Elections Act
of the president of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) and reiterate these remarks made by my colleague, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers). He said in very clear terms, and I should like to underline and repeat it, that the bill of the Progressive Conservative government, was introduced under much different circumstances. There was a minority government and an election could have been called at any moment, so it was regarded as a step that ought to be taken. Today, however, we do not contemplate a general election any earlier than two or three years hence so there is a lot of time to consider election measures. There is no comparison between what was proposed by the Progressive Conservative government and what is now taking place in this House.
It is a disservice to this House and to all members for the President of the Privy Council to get up and annoy members on this side as he always seems to do. I want to say to the President of the Privy Council, because I do not always get an opportunity to say such things to him, that if he would deal with matters with a more even and mature hand, the progress of legislation through the House would be much more even. His precipitous statements and actions are a continual annoyance to all members.
We are prepared now, and at all times, to defend our position. In this particular case it is easily defended. The problem started with the Speech from the Throne more than one year ago, when the government of which the President of the Privy Council is a member, said that it would introduce electoral reform and promised a broad-based change in the electoral provisions that apply to this nation. Where are these reforms? One year and several months later, the only electoral reform we have is Bill C-58. This is a minor change but a very important one. Without all the other changes that ought to be made, it is totally meaningless as are most of the statements made by the President of the Privy Council, to my way of thinking.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I did not mean to annoy the hon. member. If he wants to cool down, I apologize if I offended him. I did not intend to. I just ask him to keep cool and speak to the bill and we will be very happy to listen to him.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: Here we go again, Mr. Speaker. The pomposity of the hon. member who, I might say, comes from that great province where they automatically elect Liberals to the Parliament of Canada-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
-without any question of what their qualities are. I can tell you that the qualities evidenced by the hon. member in this House would not get him elected in most constituencies in Canada. Let him stay in his seat. We have heard enough from him. He has disrupted this House on too many occasions.
Now I shall speak to the bill, Mr. Speaker. The main force and thrust of this bill is very simply a change in the period of time that will elapse between the call of the election and the

June 23, 1981
Canada Elections Act
election day. Specifically, the government proposes to reduce the period from 60 days to 47 days. When we consider the public interest, we can hardly argue with that change because the people of Canada are sick of elections. They are sick of hearing the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) make promise after promise and not keep any. They heard him speak against wage and price controls and then saw him introduce them in this House. They heard him talk about lowering the price of gasoline and keeping it at a proper level and then saw the price of a gallon of gasoline rise beyond any level that any government ever proposed. In that sense, the people of Canada are sick of elections and I can understand that. If they are sick of elections, we can all understand that they would want the period of the election reduced from 60 days to 47 days.
What is the point of the reduction, Mr. Speaker? There are other ways that we could foreclose and cut off the speeches by people like the Prime Minister who promise things that they do not intend to deliver. There are other ways of achieving that, which are different from cutting down the period from 60 days to 47 days. If the President of the Privy Council does not know that, when I am sure the hon. member for Red Deer would be pleased to take him aside and, with his mature wisdom, tell that young man from the province of Quebec that there are other ways to do these things. We do not need to cut down the period of time in which a citizen who aspires to become a member of the Parliament of Canada, may present himself to the public.
What the public is concerned with is the advertising on radio and television. All of that could be cut out without reducing the period that elapses between the call of the election and polling day. I am very disappointed that the President of the Privy Council does not know that.
He asks why this bill should not go through as it is non-partisan, and he points out that it was introduced by the Progressive Conservative government. He should know that it flowed from the bureaucracy. The Chief Electoral Officer sat down one day and decided that he did not like the 60 days and that he was going to write a report and recommend a shorter period. That is very nice for the Chief Electoral Officer but I do not think he wants to become a member of Parliament. There may be people in the country who do and they may need more than 47 days to campaign. It is nice that the Chief Electoral Officer has given some thought to the subject and made a report, but that does not mean that we have to accept his word on the subject.
If we in this Parliament feel that there are other points that ought to be taken into consideration, then that is what we ought to do. We ought not to blindly follow the views expressed by the Chief Electoral Officer, whether or not they are endorsed by the President of the Privy Council.
What is the point of reducing the length of a campaign? The change would really cut down on the campaign techniques and methods that may be used, but there are many other ways that this could be done.
I have reviewed the history of this proposed change and have already indicated that the suggestion came from the Chief
Electoral Officer who made a report in December, 1975. Interestingly enough, his major concern was the cost of printing the preliminary lists of electors which he said at that time would cost about $4 million. Now, in April, May and June of 1981, the Government of Canada is going to reduce the expenditures of the country by $4 million! Thanks a lot to all those taxpayers who have contributed $60 billion to the Government of Canada to spend on all of those programs which they think Canadians need. The government will reduce that by $4 million, so we will not spend $60 billion, we will spend only $59.9 billion and some odd million. I am sure the people of Canada will be duly grateful. What they may not be grateful for is the amount of time in which they have to consider which candidates and which party they ought to elect to the House of Commons. That is what they may not thank you for. Why would they not thank you for that? As those who run for office know, a certain amount of time is needed for candidates to introduce themselves to the electorate, to deal with the issues and to conduct their campaign. It does not mean that they have to be featured on TV. It does not mean they have to advertise in newspapers, periodicals and so on. All of that can be controlled. But why limit the period of time? That is the point of this bill.
The President of the Privy Council, that great man from the province of Quebec who comes here and tells us how to conduct elections, is the one who says we need this reduction in time. I have just one question. How does he know that we Canadians need this reduction in the period of time? Does he know what the situation is in Bow River? Does he know what the situation is in the Yukon? Does he know what the situation is in Prince Edward Island? What in heavens name does he know? Has he even travelled to those places? I have never seen him in Halifax, Nova Scotia. Have you seen him out west? No, but he knows. He is like all of those people over there. Some magical process tells them that they know. They have received a mandate from the people of Canada and they know what to do about all those situations. They know how to handle them. They know what to do. That is grand. But I do not have that kind of arrogance. I do not have that kind of pomposity which tells me I know what is good for the people of Canada.
I say if you have a provision in the statutes of the Parliament of Canada which affects all the people of Canadas, like the Canada Elections Act does, you have to be very careful about changing it. It is nice that the Chief Electoral Officer has looked at it and said, "We can save money by shortening the period." That is very good and that is a point in their favour.
How far has the government gone? Has the government consulted with the people? Has the government asked the people whether they want the period of elections shortened? I do not think the government has done anything like that. I think people have sat in the back rooms of government and made this decision for the people of Canada.

I am here to say without any trepidation that I reject that. If the government can tell me that the people of Canada want this change, I would be the first to join with the government to support this bill. The government has not done that. The government has not vetted this provision. The government has not asked the people of Canada, and the government does not know whether or not this change is desired across Canada. What is more important, the government has had all kinds of time to ask the people of Canada. The government can do it with the electoral reform commissions promised in the Speech from the Throne over a year ago. This promise has not been delivered. The government has all kinds of time and resources. The government can go across this country and ask the people of Canada what they want in the way of electoral reform. The simple question can be asked: do you want this period reduced or not? Why would the people of Canada want the period reduced? They want to see the candidates. They want to see the leaders. They want to hear the comments. They want to consider all of the factors that go into making up the vote in an election. Therefore, let us consult with the people. Let us take our time. Let us not get carried away with a bill that was introduced in the House of Commons a year or two ago by another government, recommended by the Chief Electoral Officer. Who the heck cares about the Chief Electoral Officer? Who is he? He is one man.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: He was appointed.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
There is the word, he was appointed by this House. He is not appointed by the people of Canada. Anytime we have the opportunity to consult with the people of Canada on the issue, which is an issue which belongs to the people, that is their issue and, that is what we should do. We should never rely on one man, be he Chief Electoral Officer, Mr. Speaker, or the President of the Privy Council, particularly with the attitude that man has who holds that office.
The government has promised electoral reform. No one asked the government for electoral reform. There was not a plebiscite; there was not a referendum. The government in the Speech from the Throne offered the people of Canada electoral reform. The government comes up with Bill C-58, which merely reduces the time that elapses between the issuance of the writ and the date of the election and makes the other mechanical actions, the preparation of the voters lists and so on, conform with that period of time.
Let me tell the government and the President of the Privy Council about some aspects of electoral reform. What about the number of seats following an election? What is the government going to do about that? Is that going to be put aside or put off to another day while we deal with this minor electoral reform? What about the financial provisions? Are the government and the people of Canada satisfied with that? Are they not concerned with the party that can produce the most money and win the most seats? Is this not a factor that should be vetted? What about swearing in urban voters? If you live in the city and are not on the voters list, you do not get the
Canada Elections Act
notice, and if you do not get the notice, you do not know that you are not on the voters list and you lose your right to vote. What are you going to do about urban voters and swearing them in during an election? Why would there be this discrimination and discrepancy between urban and rural voters? All of us in this Parliament support not the urban voters and not the rural voters, but the voters of Canada. We all think they should have equal rights. What is the government going to do about that? Let us see a bill dealing with that subject.
What about two enumerators in urban polls? How much would it cost? It is 282 times whatever it costs for an urban voter. The people of Canada spend that amount of money, but in rural areas they do not need to. They need only one enumerator. Who made that decision? I do not think the member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) had any part in that decision. I do not think most members in this House had any part in that decision. Surely that is a matter we should look at and reconsider. We should question whether it is right or proper to have two urban enumerators and one rural enumerator. Where is your bill on that, Mr. President of the Privy Council?
What about time of voting from east to west? What a ludicrous provision that is. You can turn on your radio in British Columbia and find out three hours before you vote what the result is in eastern Canada, Nova Scotia and now half an hour earlier in Newfoundland. We all know about that. What are you doing about that? Is that right? Should a person in British Columbia know in advance what the vote is? What about time? Are you going to do anything about that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am sorry that I have to interrupt the hon. member because he seems to be quite wound up this evening. I was going to call for relevance but there is a point that I think is quite valid. There is a bill before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections dealing with the electoral clock. My understanding of the rules tells me that it is improper for an hon. member to talk about a matter which is currently before another forum of this House.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: I am sure the parliamentary secretary is referring to the rule of relevancy. I am sure that members of his House appreciate and accept the fact that the rules have been stretched quite a bit, especially on this bill, by all members. The bill is very narrow in scope. At the beginning of the debate I invited members to keep their discussion to the shortening of the election period. However, there has been argument from both sides stretching parts of the bill. It is a matter of members criticizing the bill and saying that another bill should be before the House. I think that is what the hon. member was doing.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
The government members are hurting over a few remarks I made. I do not speak that often in this House. It is reassuring that I can get to them in that way. Obviously if I were just palavering and swarming over these provisions and

Canada Elections Act
wasting time, they would not get up. However, they are hurting. They do not want these reforms that I have listed. They do not want to deal with the time of voting, the official count, two enumerators, swearing in urban voters, financial positions and the number of seats in the House of Commons, so I will pass over that. I will not embarrass them further with that. Let me just say this in conclusion. This bill, as I said at the outset, reduces the election period, but it does it in a way that is discriminating between the voters of Canada. Why? Because it continues that difference between urban voters and rural voters.
That ought not to happen. Why? Because those members across the way who are so certain of their position in relation to the electorate of Canada, so sure that they are the guardians of the rights of the people of Canada, have guaranteed a right to the people of Canada, that is the right that every citizen has the right to vote in an election of members of the House of Commons. They put that in the Canadian charter of rights and freedoms which they put through this House with all the power and authority of a majority government but without the consent and concurrence of the people of Canada.
The government says that everybody has the right to vote. Then what does it do? With the Canada Elections Act and this amendment the government says it is a little different, it is not exactly just the right to vote, but the right to vote in a certain way in an urban area and a right to vote in a certain way in a rural area. If you live in an urban area, you can only vote if you are registered and get on the list, but if you live in a rural area and can get on the list after. Therefore, the charter of rights that the government brought before the House of Commons and across Canada to make everybody equal is not going to make them equal just like that. It is going to be a little equal and different.
That is what the government is bringing before this House. It is going to perpetuate the difference that now exists even though the whole thrust and purpose of the constitutional resolution is to remove differences and to remove discrimination. There is no intention of removing discrimination, and the electoral law is one example. The government does not intend to remove discrimination for handicapped persons or with regard to regional disparities. It is all window dressing. The government in interested in fooling the people of Canada. It fooled them once on wage and price controls and it fooled them once on gasoline prices. It wants to fool them again on election provisions, but we are here to stop that.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member will permit a question. I know he will because he is a very wise man. speechtext:
I am glad the President of the Privy Council has asked me that question. I have a summary here of all the election periods right across Canada. They go from 28 to 35 and beyond. What I want to say to the President of the Privy
Council is that it is the date that the people of Canada think is appropriate after they consider all the factors and a general electoral reform under the auspices of the kind of commission and committee that the government proposed in its Speech from the Throne. What I say very simply so that he can understand is: let him consult the people of Canada. They will tell him what period of time is appropriate. He does not need to ask us or anybody else.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must first apologize to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) for the demotion I gave him when I referred to him as parliamentary secretary. I can understand the minister's rush to bring in Bill S-6 because it is legally binding upon the government to pay an additional $ 125 million to farmers in the Canadian Wheat Board area. As long as it sits there, the government is encumbered by that. Therefore, I can understand his concern that it be brought forward quickly.
I would like in the time allotted to me to address briefly members who do not have large rural ridings. Members from metro areas can go into an apartment block with a team and spend most of the afternoon there. My constituency measures
18,000	square miles. It is not the largest in Canada. Some members in the government benches and some of my colleagues have larger constituencies.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: You better believe it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
I hear some bemoaning the fact that theirs are larger. In a constituency structured like mine in rural Saskatchewan, there are no large centres. About every 12 miles there is a village of 40 to 50 people. Occasionally you come across a larger village of 500 people. Therefore, unlike the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields), the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) and the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), I cannot fly from point to point. There is no point in flying six or 12 miles. In that type of constituency it is necessary that members travel by road in order to communicate with the voters.
As an incumbent members of Parliament, I guess I should welcome this bill. In a constituency structured like mine, it offers a large advantage over someone wanting to become known. I will give just a little bit of history. I began campaigning in 1978 for the 1979 election. I had as opponents a member of Parliament who had been defeated in 1974, and a newly nominated candidate.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROPOSAL TO CONSTRUCT PRODUCTION CENTRE IN TORONTO
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROPOSAL TO CONSTRUCT PRODUCTION CENTRE IN TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, May 15, 1981, when the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation appeared before the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, I renewed my question concerning the CBC plans to build a production centre in Toronto. Mr. Johnson's reply was as follows:
That until there is an indication of a commitment of funds from the government for the construction of the Toronto broadcasting facility, which would be the equivalent of the one that was built in Montreal quite some time ago, we frankly have not been committing funds. There just is no money in the budget for Toronto consolidation and I am unable to predict to you when that money will be made available by government.
One week later, on Friday, May 22, 1981, I pursued the same subject with the government when I rose in the House to ask the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) what steps his department has taken, or plans to take, toward the construction of a Toronto production centre. The reply I received was that:
It is up to the CBC to make recommendations to cabinet.
Thus we unfortunately have the present situation where both the federal government and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are shunning the responsibility to each other on who is exactly responsible for the long overdue establishment of a production centre in Toronto similar to those already in operation in Montreal, Vancouver and the one soon to be established in Regina.
Before I pursue this matter again in the House I would like to add some facts of which I assume most Canadians are not aware.
During my recent tour of the 23 CBC buildings in Toronto at 19 different sites, I found the conditions and facilities to be absolutely appalling. To even think of the millions of dollars spent each and every year renovating these buildings with accoustics, lighting and other necessities is enough to give one indigestion. Can you just imagine the nightmare and waste of valuable manpower running from one building to another with tapes and scripts? It is a real struggle to co-ordinate the services of the CBC in Toronto with these facilities spread over such a large physical setting.
Further, it must be noted that the present situation, difficult as it is, is becoming much worse, especially when one considers that three-quarters of the space presently occupied by the CBC in Toronto is leased, and much of this rental accommodation is to come up for renewal. Given the present market
Adjournment Debate
conditions for rental space in downtown Toronto there is little doubt, if any, that the new rental leases will be sky high.
How is the CBC expected to develop or even maintain high quality programs when more and more of its budget is being eroded by rental expenses? Put simply, the CBC has become a victim of the marketplace where increases in budget are not keeping up with the increases in recent expenses, thus forcing many of the facilities into second and third-rate rental space, further away from each building.
I am not here to advocate a mere building to house all of the CBC's facilities in Toronto under one roof. Rather, I am here to urge the government and Canadians to develop the concept of establishing a world class broadcasting centre in Toronto on a 9.5 acre site adjacent to the CN Tower, presently owned by the CBC. This is a reality which would physically and symbolically meet the CBC's production needs as a world leader in radio and television broadcasting, as well as signal an international identity to the world in the fact that Canada celebrates its cultural wealth in architectural design, technology, production, craftsmanship, arts, innovation and imagination.
Toronto and Canada have many of the world's finest writers, producers and performers, and to deny Canadians this celebration is to deny them the cultivation of our human creative resources and culture.
It is here that I would like to drive home another concept, that is that, as Canadians we should not limit our options to traditional government capital expenditures of money. Rather, we should be exploring options and possibilities for the marriage of both public and private enterprises in bringing about this realization and celebration of the Canadian cultural dream.
Let me return to some of my earlier statements this evening. When I put the question in the House to the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications, "What is the government planning to do about such a facility?", the answer I received from him was that it is up to the CBC to decide whether or not it wants to build such a facility. When I asked that question of the CBC, it pawned off the responsibility to the government, and when I asked it of the government, it pawned off the responsibility to the CBC.
Therefore, I would like to know tonight once and for all just who is responsible for making that decision, when will it be made and what are the costs involved? If it is too costly to begin construction immediately, then surely we as Canadians should be putting so much aside each year so that two years, three years, or even five years down the line we will have the necessary elements and the necessary capital put together to build a CBC production centre in Toronto similar to the kind that Montreal, Vancouver and Regina boast.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Ursula Appolloni (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROPOSAL TO CONSTRUCT PRODUCTION CENTRE IN TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has its main English language facilities located in some 22 different buildings scattered across Toronto, some of which are badly substandard. Over the years,

June 23, 1981
Adjournment Debate
the CBC has imaginatively overcome some of the compromises of this situation. However, the optimum solution has long been recognized as being a consolidation of facilities. In fact, the CBC purchased a prime site on Front Street in 1978 and developed plans for a consolidation.
As the minister has stated, estimates for the construction of a new CBC facility on this site range from $235 million to $250 million, which by any standard is a considerable sum of money. A capital outlay of this magnitude must be considered in relation to the total level of CBC's parliamentary appropriation, which includes some $60 million for capital projects. As hon. members know, the CBC is required by Parliament to serve all Canadians, which it does according to an independent evaluation, with a level of efficiency which exceeds that of most other state-operated broadcasting services in other countries.
With this in mind, one could ask whether the CBC could devote the entirety of its capital budget to a single major project, such as a consolidation of Toronto facilities, and still maintain the same level of excellent service across Canada. I think it is clear that CBC management is doing its utmost to balance its obligation to provide both a high level of regional programming as well as quality radio and television programming for national audiences.
To enhance the CBC's ability to "serve the special needs of geographic regions", as the Broadcasting Act directs, the government has recently approved a new CBC broadcast facility for Regina, Saskatchewan. This major facility, to be located in the Wascana Centre, will entail three television studios, nine radio studios, plus associated production and administrative areas. It is a project which will cost over $16 million and will significantly improve the corporation's English and French radio and TV service in that province. Similarly, in Newfoundland the government has approved the construction of a new broadcast facility for Grand Falls.
Meanwhile, as a fellow Torontonian I share the hon. member's concern for the difficult circumstances under which the CBC now operates in our city. Currently, the CBC must lease the majority of its Toronto accommodation. As the hon. member stated, the economic situation is different now from what it was a short time ago. The cost of rental accommodation in Toronto is going up and terms for lease agreements are becoming shorter. The CBC is naturally concerned about this situation and has been exploring possible solutions.
Therefore, the CBC recently approached the government with a proposal to lease new facilities in Toronto. The intent of this project is to consolidate under one roof some of the activities presently undertaken at separate locations in the city such as editing facilities, variety production, computing facilities, etc. I think it goes without saying that a higher degree of physical proximity will aid operational efficiency of those units involved. Secondly, it will enable the CBC to vacate some of its current premises which are substandard. Clearly, it is with these objectives in mind that the government has approved this new undertaking which, at least for the immediate future, will facilitate CBC's operations in Toronto which are so vital both
to the service it provides in southern Ontario and to much of the English language programming seen and heard nationally.

subtopic: HOUSING-(A) MEASURES TO HELP HOME OWNERS FACING

speechtext: INCREASED MORTGAGE PAYMENTS; (B) SUPPORT FOR CO-OP PROJECTS; (C) BANKS' PROFITS ON PROPERTY TAX COMPONENT OF MORTGAGE PAYMENTS

subtopic: HOUSING-(A) MEASURES TO HELP HOME OWNERS FACING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you do not know how I have to fight off the temptation to give the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis) some additional information about CBC that the departmental answer did not provide. However, I have to go on to the question that I have.
It concerns questions I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a week ago regarding social housing. June is the month when probably half the mortgages in Canada will be renewed, and CMHC estimates there will be 500,000 thousands mortgages renewed in Canada this year. That affects about two million people, Mr. Speaker, and I think it would be conservative to estimate that the mortgage payments will increase anywhere from 30 per cent to 45 per cent and more for those families.
This means the mortgage payments on their houses will increase by $300 to $400 per month, which is the equivalent of their grocery budgets. But their salaries have not increased to meet this, so the squeeze will be on them. I might add that this affects all families from the young ones to senior citizens.
I asked the Prime Minister about social housing or the development of co-operative housing. A developer told me not long ago that the best deal for low-income families today was co-operative housing. When a developer tells me this, I know there is a serious problem in the housing industry, particularly in the greater Vancouver area. The Prime Minister fluffed off that one too.
Just last week I talked with a person who was trying to negotiate a project which would provide housing for handicapped low and middle-income families in the south Surrey-White Rock area, but the minister had already declared that the greater Vancouver area would not get more housing units this year. Thus, there was no sense in even trying to negotiate a project which was vitally needed in the area. The Prime Minister did not want to intervene on that one either.
Finally I asked the Prime Minister about the policy of banks and large lending institutions in Canada whereby they collect the money for property taxes as part of the mortgage payments. I have no quarrel with that arrangement; I have done it for many years. It is a good arrangement for home owners- while they make their mortgage payments, they pay extra money each month to pay for their property taxes. The banks offer a good service to home owners which enables them to make the property tax payments.
Something which I had not noticed before came to my attention last week. The banks pay 3 per cent on the property
June 23, 1981

tax component of the mortgage payment. Property owners do not have to do it through the banks. They can set up their own trust accounts and do it on the side, but the banks do not advertise this very thoroughly and most of the time property owners assume that it is part of the procedure. Again I say it is a good service, I have no quarrel with it, except that the banks are paying 3 per cent. This is less than 20 per cent of the going rate. I think the parliamentary secretary will agree that one can now get 16 per cent to 17.5 per cent on a certificate, yet banks are paying only 3 per cent on the property tax component of mortgage payments.
If one million mortgages are being held by the banks on which they are collecting the property tax component, and if we cut in half the $1,000 or $2,000 they are collecting in property taxes to arrive at the average amount they are holding on behalf of property owners, we arrive at $500 million at 3 per cent. Therefore the banks are paying out to property owners $15 million per year. However, if they paid the going rate or even 15 per cent, which is below the going rate, they would be required to pay $75 million. This means that the banks made unearned profits of $60 million, which is a very low estimate, on the mortgages they are holding for property owners.
As I said the other day, it is unconscionable. The Prime Minister said that he would refer the matter to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and that the Minister of Finance would go to the banks and the lending institutions to make representations to them on that matter. I guess the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bockstael) will read the departmental answer tonight. Am I correct?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: HOUSING-(A) MEASURES TO HELP HOME OWNERS FACING
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: HOUSING-(A) MEASURES TO HELP HOME OWNERS FACING
speechtext: I wish to know two things, Mr. Speaker. First, did the Prime Minister refer that matter to the Minister of Finance and, in turn, did the Minister of Finance make a representation to the national banks? Second, what have the banks said, if in fact that has happened? What answer have those banks given to the Minister of Finance? Will they stop ripping off the property owners who are facing enough of a squeeze as a result of the escalation in mortgage payments? Will home owners receive some kind of return on the dollars invested which will be in some way relevant to the kind of payments being made on all other kinds of savings accounts, loans certificates etc? What does the parliamentary secretary have to say? Has that representation been made?

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: HOUSING-(A) MEASURES TO HELP HOME OWNERS FACING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment further on the matters raised by the hon. member on June 17.
With respect to the home owners who face possible foreclosure because of increased mortgage payments due to high interest rates, I should like to point out that the lending industry has indicated to both the minister and his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), a willingness to bend over backward to help those experiencing serious difficul-
Adjournment Debate
ties in meeting their mortage payments on renewal. I believe such cases can and are being given sympathetic consideration by the lenders. It is, after all, in their interest to avoid foreclosure.
As I have indicated, Mr. Speaker, last year the federal government extended assistance to home owners who received contributions when they bought their houses in 1975 under the Assisted Home Ownership Program, known as AHOP. In March of this year the government agreed to continue to apply the extended assistance to qualifying AHOP home owners. The maximum amount available to a home owner is $1,500 a year, up from last year's limit of $750.
In response to the hon. member's query and support for co-op projects, I agree that this form of housing has proven to be an effective way of providing adequate and affordable family housing. Last year the federal government allocated
5,000	social housing units for municipalities experiencing an acute shortage of rental accommodation. The minister is looking into the feasibility of increasing the unit allocation to such tight market locations this year.
The hon. member raised the question of profits made by banks on the property tax component of mortgage payments. 1 should like to point out that the mortgage form prescribed by the national housing loan regulations requires approved lenders under the National Housing Act to pay property taxes on behalf of borrowers. Officials of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation are presently reviewing the problem that current interest rates have created with respect to the interest allowable on tax deposits provided for in NHA mortgages, with a view to determining if this policy should be revised.

subtopic: MARINE TRANSPORT-WITHDRAWAL OF DART CONTAINERLINE SERVICE FROM HALIFAX-DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT
MARINE TRANSPORT-WITHDRAWAL OF DART CONTAINERLINE SERVICE FROM HALIFAX-DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter I wish to raise this evening relates back to February and March of 1981. It concerns the decision of the Dart shipping group to move its container service from the Port of Halifax to the Port of Montreal in connection with a proposed liaison between the Dart shipping group and Canadian Pacific Limited.
In specific terms, on March 4, 1981, I questioned the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) with respect to the involvement of the Canadian National Railway Company in the operations of the Cast shipping group, which I considered, and which many in the Port of Halifax considered, to be interinvolved with the decision of the Dart shipping group to remove its operation to the Port of Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, one of the problems which has occurred in the last few years in relation to the North Atlantic container traffic is the competition which has driven many of the marine transportation companies out of business. It is apparent that there has been a consolidation of the marine transport service amongst a few international operators. One of these international operators is the organization which is apparently headed

Adjournment Debate
by a Canadian citizen who lives abroad, and who operates the Cast shipping group.
The decision of the Canadian National Railway Company, endorsed by the Government of Canada, to invest over $60 million in the Cast shipping group, has given the impression to the international marine transport companies that the Cast shipping group has the backing of the Canadian government. It was only reasonable then that the Dart shipping group, as well as other international marine transport companies, would seek to protect themselves from this kind of special deal which was provided by the Government of Canada through its agency, the Canadian National Railway Company.
Therefore, with that motivation in mind, the province of Nova Scotia, and other persons who were interested in the port of Halifax, sought the assistance of the Minister of Transport in reviewing the decision which was made by the Dart group and the Canadian Pacific Railway whereby the container service was removed, as I have said, from the port of Halifax to the port of Montreal. In specific terms, what the premier of the province of Nova Scotia asked the Minister of Transport to do was to hold an inquiry at which all of the factors which were relevant to this kind of decision-making would be reviewed.
The Minister of Transport indicated in this House of Commons and elsewhere that the whole matter could be reviewed by the Canadian Transport Commission at a hearing which was required under the National Transportation Act, because Canadian Pacific Limited, being a transport company, sought to acquire an interest in Dart.
That hearing was held last week in the city of Halifax; but unfortunately, at the very outset of the hearing it was stated in categorical terms by the representative of the Canadian Pacific Limited, that nothing will stop Dart's move to the port of Montreal. Consequently, Nova Scotians, from the premier of Nova Scotia right across to those interested in the port of Halifax and all citizens, were very disappointed because there was no way that this whole decision could be reviewed.
We have repercussions because in the U.S. Congress and before a committee of the United States Congress objections have been raised to the operation of the Cast shipping group. It has been described as a James Bond company, robbing traffic from U.S. marine carriers and taking them to Canadian ports. On the face of it, there might seem to be some advantages for Canada; but after all, we are a very small country dealing with the United States goliath.
I can guarantee Your Honour and all hon. members of this House that if the United States retaliates against these predatory moves by the Cast shipping group, which are said to have the support of the Government of Canada, and are said in that congressional hearing to be a flag carrier of Canada, it will be a disaster for the Canadian marine industry. It will be a disaster because the United States has that kind of power, so much so that our Canadian embassy had to send a diplomatic note asking that a bill proposed by the Congress of the United States to enact these measures which would protect the U.S. marine industry be delayed and not passed by the Congress.
This is the kind of problem that arises from the government's involvement. Encouraging Dart to move from the port of Halifax to the port of Montreal not only affects the port of Halifax, it has international repercussions as well. If allegations have been made, they must be answered by the Minister of Transport. The only way they can be properly answered is at a full hearing. We can review the whole marine transportation industry in relation to container traffic and get the answers-not only the answers necessary to protect the port of Halifax from the predatory moves of the port of Montreal, but also the answers that will stave off the criticism now being vented in the United States and which could have very serious repercussions.
The Minister of Transport has a serious obligation in this area. I can understand how he would seek to protect the port of Montreal by writing off $230 million in debts and by providing millions of dollars worth of infrastructure for that port, but by doing so he is going to create an international controversy and wreak havoc in the marine industry in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MARINE TRANSPORT-WITHDRAWAL OF DART CONTAINERLINE SERVICE FROM HALIFAX-DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 4 the hon. member asked the minister what he would do to equalize the treatment of the ports of Halifax and Montreal. At that time, and on several subsequent occasions in the House, the minister tried to show that it is impossible to demonstrate that one port is favoured over another. For each example of an advantage for Montreal, one can easily cite an advantage for Halifax.
I can understand the hon. member's reasons for bringing this issue up again. He has just attended hearings by the Canadian Transport Commission into CP's acquisition of one third of Dart Containerline. Given that the CTC has not yet rendered a decision, it would not be appropriate to comment on the submissions.
But I think that, in his concern for the port of Halifax, he has lost sight of the fundamental commercial reality of the situation. Dart and CP arranged this deal so that they could begin using larger, more fuel-efficient container ships in their service to Europe. He claims that government policies caused the move from Halifax. I suggest that government policies were quite incidental to the move, and in any case, it cannot be proven that the port of Montreal is favoured.
The minister made it quite clear that interested parties had several opportunities to state their cases. In Halifax last week, the hon. member had one such opportunity. It will be up to the CTC to determine if his intervention was relevant.
In a previous answer, the minister stated that the Premier of Nova Scotia and all other interested parties would have three opportunities to bring the subject forward in the coming months. Under section 33 of the act they could have an inquiry into the acquisition by CP ships of part of the Dart Company, and under section 27 of the act they could intervene if the CN should decide to increase its ownership of CAST in the coming
June 23, 1981

months. There are two, and possibly three opportunities for members and the Premier of Nova Scotia to make an intervention on the subject of freight rates that he contends will be increased by the CNR.
Rather than painting a dark picture of his home town, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should be promoting it. He should be describing the active marketing of the port by Halterm and Ceres. He should be noting the new transshipment arrangements in Halifax by a large Puerto Rican line, and he should
Adjournment Debate
be announcing that the Polish ocean line, a new caller at the port, intends to double its visits to Halifax, starting in 1982. That is the sort of news that will give Halifax the good name it deserves!
